text:
From the Mexican restaurant where he works in North Austin, Juan Perez has seen U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers detain more and more people in the area.

That includes construction workers, stopping at the gas station or the Dollar Tree for ice before their work day begins. And lone drivers, whose cars are left unattended after they’re hauled away. On Saturday, Perez saw one guy taken away. On Thursday, another man, trying to flee, ran through the restaurant’s parking lot. Perez did not see if ICE caught him.

“It’s been going on for a month here and they’ve just been — respectfully — terrorizing the whole area,” Perez, 28, said as he looked past a mostly empty restaurant and onto the street on Monday. “I just guess they’re easy targets because a lot of people, a lot of construction people gotta put gas or whatever in the mornings.”

The restaurant sits among a group of small businesses near the intersection where an ICE officer on Sunday shot and wounded Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old immigrant from Venezuela. To some in the area, a violent encounter was all but inevitable as they have seen federal agents — often in unmarked cars, sometimes accompanied by Texas Department of Public Safety troopers — pick up the pace of their hunting for immigrants.

“It’s just sad,” Perez said, shaking his head. “If you were just going after rapists … I understand that. But I mean, you’re going after hardworking people.”

The shooting occurred amid a surge of ICE activity in Austin that is injecting fear into Latino residents, citizens and undocumented alike, according to others who work in the area, local activists and elected officials from Austin City Hall to Congress.

Garces Perez’s violent arrest has placed a spotlight on the soaring number of ICE arrests, and renewed scrutiny on the willingness of Texas’ GOP leaders to help President Donald Trump pursue his mass deportation campaign.

ICE has divided Texas into five jurisdictions, and street arrests in the San Antonio jurisdiction, which includes Austin, have skyrocketed since the beginning of the year, according to a Texas Tribune analysis.

Since 2022, when the practice of apprehending undocumented people in the interior of the country was far less common under the Biden administration, the San Antonio jurisdiction has seen a 32.2-point increase in field-based arrests — one of the largest jumps in the country, the data review shows.

“It’s ‘Hey, Mexican, come here,’ type of enforcement,” Austin City Council member Chito Vela, whose district includes the site of Garces Perez’s shooting, said of the increased ICE presence. “We’re talking about gas stations and, you know, parking lots of grocery stores — that kind of like really random enforcement of immigration laws that we have seen over the last 30 days.”

Mario Tapia launched a magazine 12 years ago for Latinos in Central Texas. Since Trump returned to the White House, he has been publishing videos of ICE arrests on Instagram. He said the earliest videos he received from followers in April 2025 were difficult to initially confirm as ICE arrests because the officers drove unmarked cars and wore vests that simply said “police.”

But soon it became clear that the authorities were from ICE, he said, as more videos emerged, followed by accounts from relatives of those detained. He said he has documented two types of arrests during Trump’s second term: some are initiated by DPS traffic stops, with troopers calling ICE if they confirm the person they pulled over is undocumented, while others are solo ICE pursuits, like the one that led to Garces Perez’s shooting.

Tapia said most of the reports he receives are from North Austin, including the site of the shooting.

“I understand this subject polarizes a lot of people,” he said Monday. “But I wish people would notice what this all means not just for the undocumented immigrant community, but in general for the entire Hispanic community. There’s fear.”

Texas has played a starring role in the president’s immigration crackdown. Shortly after Trump’s return to Washington, Gov. Greg Abbott directed DPS — and other state agencies — to help the federal government. After years of patrolling the U.S.-Mexico border as part of Abbott’s Operation Lone Star initiative, the state agency has redirected some resources from the border to assist ICE in the interior of the state.

As of Monday evening, top Texas GOP officials — including the governor and the lieutenant governor — had yet to weigh in publicly on Garces Perez’s shooting.

The increased ICE presence has put people on edge across the state capital.

Austin City Council member Zohaib “Zo” Qadri, whose district covers central Austin, said his office has received reports from University of Texas at Austin students when they see something that makes them suspicious.

“The governor has weaponized DPS to kinda go around and terrorize folks in Austin,” Qadri said. “The president has, you know, weaponized ICE to go around and terrorize folks in Austin.”

Sulma Franco, the director of immigration campaigns at the Austin nonprofit Grassroots Leadership, said her group has also seen an uptick in immigration arrests on Austin’s streets since Trump’s return to office.

“It’s terrible that Texas is turning into a laboratory for these racist laws,” she said. “It’s frustrating to see our community in constant fright.”

Maria Elizabeth has witnessed the fear. The 30-year-old works at a restaurant behind a convenience store that serves Latin American cuisine, down the street from where ICE shot Garces Perez.

“People don’t want to stop by,” Elizabeth said. “They’re scared of the police, they’re scared of ICE.”

On Monday afternoon, the picnic tables near the counter were empty. Down the street, people began leaving candles and other objects to mark where Garces Perez was shot.

Sam Stark of the Austin Current contributed to this report.

text:
A Venezuelan man who was wounded Sunday when an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shot him is back in the hospital and asking a court to intervene before he can be removed from the country.

The man, identified as 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, was delivering orders for DoorDash at the time of the confrontation, his attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch said. This is the latest shooting incident involving the agency since the Trump administration started its immigration crackdown.

Federal authorities haven’t said what led to the shooting of Garces Perez, who was taken to a hospital Monday evening after earlier being detained at the South Texas ICE Processing Center, according to his attorney. She also filed a petition in federal court Monday asking a judge to block the government from deporting Garces Perez and release him from custody while his case is pending.

The local district attorney called for an independent investigation into what happened.

This is at least the third shooting involving immigration agents in Texas since President Donald Trump started his second term, and is part of a larger trend of shootings by federal agents since stricter immigration enforcement began.

At least 20 people have been shot by on-duty ICE and US Customs and Border Protection agents during the second Trump administration, eight fatally, prior to Sunday, according to a CNN analysis.

Here is what we know so far about the latest shooting:

Venezuelan man shot in North Austin by immigration agent

Garces Perez was driving in North Austin on Sunday when he was shot in the torso just before 1 p.m., officials said.

DoorDash said he was working as a Dasher at the time of the shooting.

ICE officers were conducting targeted immigration enforcement operations Sunday based on license plate checks when they came across a vehicle registered to Garces Perez, who had a deportation order, according to a source familiar with the incident.

Officers conducted a vehicle stop and questioned Garces Perez, who had a brief exchange with the officers before he fled the scene in his car, the source said. They told him they were ICE agents and that he was going to be arrested; Garces Perez then fled the scene in his car, the source said.

It is unclear whether Garces Perez’s car came to a complete stop or was moving during the initial exchange. The shooting happened later.

During a news conference Monday, Garces Perez called in from ICE custody and gave his own account of the shooting with the help of an interpreter.

Garces Perez said the SUV tried to hit him, which he originally interpreted as an aggressive driver. When he realized ICE agents were in the vehicle, Garces Perez said he asked to pull over to be detained but the federal official denied his request.

Garces Perez said when he attempted a U-turn to park the car, the SUV ran into his car and he was then shot, according to the translator.

He said after he was shot, an officer went into his car and “forcibly turned it off.” He told the officer he was in pain and felt like he was going to pass out shortly before EMTs arrived.

The Department of Homeland Security has not given a detailed account of what happened or responded to CNN’s request for comment on the circumstances of the incident.

Homeland Security Investigations, the agency’s investigative branch, will lead the investigation with assistance from the FBI, DHS said in a post on X without providing further details.

CNN reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment on Garces Perez’s account of events.

“I see ICE following their same PR pattern in this case,” Lincoln-Goldfinch told CNN on Monday. “There is no evidence to be seen that Wilber was doing anything but driving his car down the road.”

Video of the shooting was also captured by Heidi Clark, who was livestreaming to Facebook while driving down Research Boulevard. As she drove toward the intersection with Anderson Square, loud tire screeches interrupted her as she spoke.

“Woah!” Clark said as she turned her phone camera toward the scene and a person could be seen in the distance running out of an SUV toward a blue sedan.

Video from after the shooting showed a blue Toyota Corolla with damage to the front passenger door and at least two apparent bullet holes in the right rear window, according to footage shared by CNN affiliate KVUE and several witness videos taken at the scene.

Garces Perez stable but ‘not doing well’ after gunshot wound, he said

Before returning to the hospital, Garces Perez told reporters Monday that he was “not doing well” and was in a lot of pain, adding that doctors had not removed the bullet because it was too close to his spine.

“They sent him to (an ICE facility) with a bullet in his back without pain medication, and he slept overnight in a processing center without a bed,” his lawyer said.

Garces Perez also relayed, through the interpreter, that he was in a cold room with no bed at the ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, about 100 miles southwest of Austin.

Rep. Joaquin Castro of Texas said someone from his office visited Garces Perez on Monday, and reported that ICE was taking him back to the hospital as he was still reporting a lot of pain, he said in a video he posted on X.

Garces Perez has lost movement on the “entire left side of his body,” Lincoln-Goldfinch told CNN’s Erin Burnett Monday evening, which means he could be “facing paralysis.”

Later Monday, Lincoln-Goldfinch said in a video on social media that she was told by a fellow inmate that Garces Perez had been taken to a hospital. She told CNN she didn’t have an update on his condition.

CNN has reached out to DHS about his comments on his injury and the conditions of the processing center.

Video taken after the shooting and obtained by CNN shows Garces Perez sitting on a curb with his hands cuffed behind his back as he’s detained by authorities. His shirt is cut open during the video to reveal what appears to be a gaping gunshot wound in his back.

Differing accounts of legal status by DHS and attorney

DHS and Garces Perez’s attorney have different accounts about his legal status.

DHS said in a post on X that Garces Perez is an undocumented immigrant from Venezuela who had a final order for removal, adding he is stable and “in federal custody pending removal.”

But his attorney said Garces Perez entered the country on an asylum claim, where he was allowed into the country and issued a work permit. He had been protected from deportation by a parole program that included Venezuelans, which the Trump administration ended last year, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

“He had a pending court date, and the immigration court changed his court date without notifying him,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said, which ended up with Garces Perez receiving a removal order in absentia.

Lincoln-Goldfinch said she used “back channels” to find out where Garces Perez is being held. ICE recently removed the location of detainees with final removal orders from an online database, complicating their attorneys’ efforts to prevent their deportation, The Associated Press reported Monday.

Local district attorney demands independent investigation

The Travis County District Attorney’s office, which covers most of Austin, said in a statement Sunday night that “it is critical that all the facts come to light and that an independent investigation be completed.”

“We are requesting that the Austin Police Department and our office, the Travis County District Attorney, be co-equal partners in the investigation,” the statement said, and asked for access to evidence the federal government has in this case.

The statement is reminiscent of the requests the Hennepin County Attorney’s office has made in Minneapolis regarding the shooting deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti. DHS turned over some evidence to state officials last July but hasn’t released findings in their investigations.

Austin’s Democratic Mayor Kirk Watson said during a news conference Sunday that is important for the city to be involved in the investigation, adding “Austinites have a right to know what happened.”

“While I’m unhappy and I’m angry about it, I’m not surprised at all,” Watson said of the shooting. “It’s happened in other cities with the nature of ICE and the way ICE is doing its business these days.”

CNN has reached out to Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s office for comment.

The League of United Latin American Citizens, the Latino civil rights organization founded in Texas, also called on measures to curtail DHS, saying Congress should establish an independent oversight of immigration, and guarantee any DHS or ICE official who violates a person’s constitutional rights will be investigated and prosecuted, they said in a statement Sunday.

“No agency should be the sole judge of its own conduct,” Roman Palomares, LULAC chair and national president, said in a statement. “When the government takes or endangers a life, the Constitution demands due process and accountability, and those protections belong to every person in this country.”

Protests erupt in reaction to shooting

In the past several months, Texas has been at the center of the debate on immigration enforcement. In July, ICE agents fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican immigrant, in Houston during a traffic stop. ICE agents tried to conduct a traffic stop as part of a “targeted operation” and Salgado Araujo attempted to evade arrest, an agency spokesperson said in a statement to CNN at the time.

Earlier this month, two teens who are US citizens said they were attacked by ICE agents in Alamo, Texas, after they recorded an immigration stop, with video showing one being repeatedly punched in the head while pinned to the pavement. DHS told CNN in a statement at the time “two anti-ICE agitators” refused to follow verbal commands and were detained after “they attempted to obstruct officers conducting a vehicle stop.”

“This is a pattern – it’s a disturbing pattern – and it’s got to stop,” said US Rep. Greg Casar, a Democrat who represents part of Austin.

Just hours after Garces Perez was shot, protesters gathered near the busy intersection where the shooting took place. Protesters were seen lining the streets, some chanting, some holding Mexican flags.

“I’ve lived in Austin all my life, but from what I’ve been seeing right now, I’ve never felt more betrayed,” Jaasiel Avilva, a 22-year-old Army veteran and son of Mexican immigrants, told CNN. “It’s just domestic terrorism.”

Janney Olvera, 13, told CNN affiliate KEYE she and her mother went to the protest fresh from finishing cheerleading practice.

“We’re not getting any justice,” Olvera told the outlet as she held a Mexican flag to honor her Mexican and Guatemalan heritage. “This is supposed to protect our streets? I don’t think so.”

A Kentucky State University student-athlete was arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement while traveling through the Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport with the university's basketball team Aug. 7, a lawyer coordinating the student's case told The Courier Journal.

Since her arrest, Aminata Seck, 26, has been moved between at least four detention centers without consistent medical care, according to previous reporting. She is currently being held in Grayson County as of Sept. 21, according to the Grayson County Detention Center's inmate listings.

Here's what to know about the case:

Who is Aminata Seck?

Seck is a student-athlete at Kentucky State University. She joined the school's basketball team in 2024, where she plays the center position, according to KSU's 2025-26 women's basketball roster. In March, Seck was named to the Southern Intercollegiate Athletic Conference All-Conference Third Team with Elite 16 honors due to her strong academic performance.

"Seck played a key role for the team throughout the 2025-26 season, leading the squad on the boards while consistently contributing on both ends of the floor," a university report reads.

Seck transferred to KSU from Langston University, a historically Black university in Langston, Oklahoma.

"Out of respect for the privacy of those involved, Kentucky State University does not have information to share," a spokesperson for the school said in a statement to The Courier Journal.

The KSU women's basketball roster lists Seck's hometown as Dakar, Senegal.

Why was Aminata Seck taken into ICE custody?

Sadiqa Reynolds, an attorney helping coordinate Seck's case and former president and CEO of the Louisville Urban League, told The Courier Journal that Seck's team was headed to New York for a tournament when she was taken into custody after going through security at the Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport.

According to previous reporting, Reynolds said Seck may have missed a student visa deadline because she was having back surgery. Seck is currently suffering from an ACL injury, Reynolds told The Courier Journal.

What happens next in the Aminata Seck case?

Seck remains in ICE custody in Leitchfield. Reynolds previously told The Courier Journal that Seck has had trouble getting consistent access to ice for her injury and is in "so much pain."

"She needs surgery. She needs medical attention," Reynolds said in a social media post. "Kentucky State has done what they can and now we must step up."

Reynolds praised Seck's coach, Amani Williams, who she said has gone "above and beyond" advocating for her player.

"She has treated her like a mother would treat their child," Reynolds said. "I think we have to celebrate some of these heroes who have really been behind the scenes doing everything they could possibly do to keep people safe. And even though it maybe hasn't worked … nobody should have to do all of this."

Based on available court records, it is currently unclear whether Seck has filed a habeas corpus petition, a lawsuit challenging prolonged or unlawful ICE detentions.

text:
The Crestview-Wooten neighborhood, where on Sunday an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garcés Perez, wears its identity proudly. There’s a Mexican market on one block, a supermercado on the next, and paleterias, a panaderia, and Latino-owned salons and body shops nearby. It sits just south of Rundberg and the trend-resistant “Taco Mile,” named for its concentration of authentic taco joints. North Austin neighborhoods have been seeing increased ICE activity for months. Locals have reported high-speed chases, and in August, Congressman Greg Casar chastised the department for staking out schools and churches in the area.

North Austin has been under what observers call a shadow surge, and on September 20, it burst into view when an ICE agent shot Garcés Perez while he was out on a DoorDash delivery, according to his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. The agent in a black Expedition collided with the Venezuelan’s Toyota Corolla and then fired into the vehicle, striking Garcés Perez in the upper left shoulder. Witnesses say he was taken conscious from the scene.

The incident is the latest in a series of shootings by ICE agents as President Donald Trump and his advisers continue to pressure ICE to hit three thousand arrests per day. While Operation Midway Blitz, in Chicago, and Operation Metro Surge, in Minneapolis, seemed designed to draw protests and media coverage, the more-ubiquitous shadow surges across the country have been even more deadly—and disturbingly imprecise. When an ICE agent shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston in July, the Department of Homeland Security admitted that Salgado hadn’t even been the target of the stop. Six days later, an ICE agent in Maine shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, with ICE later admitting that he was also not the intended target of that operation. Reports also show that while arrests and detentions have soared to all-time highs this summer, deportations have remained level, largely because the immigrants being picked up do not have criminal records or deportation orders, or have open asylum cases.

A DHS spokesperson said in an email that Garcés Perez had “illegally entered our country under the Biden administration.” It’s not clear yet whether that means he was one of the more than 616,000 Venezuelans granted Temporary Protected Status under President Biden—a status the second Trump administration terminated—or whether he had always been in the country illegally. Much of the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement has targeted those with legal statuses granted by Biden, including legal refugee status. Lincoln-Goldfinch said her client has an open asylum case and a valid work permit.

In the Crestview neighborhood on Sunday evening, I parked my car in an empty lot next to a white pickup with a wheelbarrow and rolls of chicken wire in the bed and a bumper sticker that read “Dios es [heart].” A Latino man with a black American flag cap and work jeans greeted me with a nod. “Just getting water. You need some?” he asked as he tossed me a cold plastic bottle without waiting for the answer. He told me he worked in landscaping, was from Mexico, and was a legal permanent resident. We stood drinking our water in silence, listening to the angry shouts growing louder from the protest about a hundred feet away as Austin police officers in riot gear arrived alongside a dozen or so state troopers.

The two groups—law enforcement and protesters—stood on either side of the access road as cars honked and inched their way forward while some passengers hung out of windows. On one side was a mix of families with kids waving Mexican flags and twentysomethings in balaclavas waving middle fingers. On the other side, about two dozen officers chatted among themselves, looking relatively unbothered. A water bottle flew over the cars, aimed at the officers.

“Whew. They’re angry,” I said, looking at the protesters.

“Yes, because immigration and police,” the landscaper said, “they are almost the same thing.” He said that the previous week, he had seen a car pulled over by the police—ICE officers arrived three minutes later and took the driver away, he said.

The Austin Police Department’s relationship with immigration enforcement has changed over the past several months, and officials immediately distanced themselves from the shooting, with Chief Lisa Davis emphasizing that APD officers had not been involved but would be investigating. “This has happened in the city of Austin,” Davis said at a news conference immediately after the shooting. “The city of Austin deserves answers on what occurred.”

Tensions with local police forces cooperating with ICE are high across the state, including in Austin. In January, an APD response to a disturbance call led to ICE taking a woman and her five-year-old daughter, a U.S. citizen, into custody and later deporting them. On March 4, APD adopted new rules limiting officers’ cooperation with ICE on the civil warrants the agency issues—saying officers didn’t have to call ICE if they encountered someone with such a warrant. In mid-April, Governor Greg Abbott threatened to terminate roughly $2.5 million in state public-safety grants unless the city adjusted its new policy. About a week later, Davis announced that APD would revise the March policy, restoring a process under which officers should, when operationally feasible, contact ICE about a valid ICE-issued warrant—while still limiting how long APD could hold someone for ICE.

The nuance of to what extent APD can or cannot refuse to cooperate with ICE is difficult to discuss rationally once the PepperBalls start flying.

“You are complicit!” a protester shouted as officers headed back to their cars after securing the scene of the shooting, where a special investigations team had been working. As they backed away from the access road, some protesters rushed forward across northbound Research Boulevard, disappearing in pursuit of the officers between the stacks of concrete box culverts and utility vaults under the overpass. For a moment it looked like a scene from a dystopian film. After a few pops erupted, the crowd came sprinting back. Once everyone had regrouped—police in the parking lot of the Crestview Crossing shopping center, protesters across the street—rocks started flying. The officers formed a line, holding PepperBall guns, and fired at the curb in front of the crowd, releasing clouds of irritant. The more experienced among the protesters donned their respirators. Twenty minutes later, the police were gone, and the protest began to reorganize around the spot where Garcés Perez—by then reported to be in serious but stable condition in ICE custody at Dell Seton Medical Center—had been shot.

Over at the Crestview Crossing shopping center, it was relatively quiet, a helicopter still circling overhead. Only then did the door of the center’s paleteria open. A couple emerged, looking distressed. “I talked to him,” said the husband, aged sixty, who asked only to be identified as Carlos. “We saw where he was shot. In the back.”

Carlos had also talked to the ICE agent, he said, who told him he had shot Garcés Perez because the Venezuelan man had not stopped when the officer said to stop. “So he shot him,” Carlos repeated. “But the police don’t have nothing to do with this,” he added, gesturing at the remnants of the confrontation. He said he understood the anger and fear in the community, but he didn’t feel that screaming and throwing rocks were doing any good. “I’m scared. . . . I’m just trying to help my people, but this is not good for nobody. Nobody.”

Later, I drove to Dell Seton Medical Center to see whether anyone there had answers about Garcés Perez. Everyone—lawyers, family, press—had been kicked off the campus, I found out. DHS replied to my inquiry with an emailed statement: “The illegal alien’s condition is stable, and he is in federal custody pending removal.” The statement also said that Homeland Security Investigations and the FBI would be investigating the shooting. Lincoln-Goldfinch said her client was released from the hospital after only a few hours. This morning CBS confirmed that Garcés Perez is being held at the detention center in Pearsall, south of San Antonio.

Back at the scene of the shooting, a vigil had formed. Austinites filled the U.S. 183 underpass, mingling with cars and motorcycles in a mass of honking, tejano music, revving engines, and waving flags. Without the police presence, anger had softened into a sort of binding agent, pulling the crowd members close together, ebbing and flowing, making space for neighbors as they joined.

Someone put down a circle of tea lights and flowers around the spot where Garcés Perez fell, asking anyone with a lighter to come help. People did, and the crowd filled the street around the circle as the traffic lights blinked red overhead, marking the intersection as a place to take caution.

This was the spot where Carlos had sat with Garcés Perez until being shooed away. Carlos recalled saying to the younger man: “This is not American people, my friend. The way they are doing this, this is something else.” What that something else was, he didn’t know.

text:
In a new survey, homebuilders around the country say ramped-up Immigration and Customs Enforcement crackdowns are creating huge headaches for their businesses.

Why it matters: The labor strain comes on top of other challenges for the industry: rising mortgage rates, higher prices for key inputs driven by tariffs and the Iran war, as well as growing competition for resources with builders of data centers.

What they're saying: "ICE is becoming a very large issue and causing labor shortages," says a Houston builder in a survey conducted earlier this month by John Burns Research and Consulting, which regularly asks homebuilders about market conditions.

A builder in Richmond, Virginia, says: "ICE has had significant impacts to vendors throughout Virginia/Maryland in the last 90 days. ... This has had a major impact on cycle times and the ability to start new houses."

Jacksonville, Florida: "Current immigration enforcement efforts in our region are causing a strain on both the labor force, labor costs and cycle times."

The intrigue: The remarks in the homebuilder survey were unprompted, says Rick Palacios, director of research at the consulting firm.

"All we asked about on the topic in our survey was construction cycle times," he says. "The comments on 'ICE and immigration' were completely unsolicited."

Zoom in: The strains come after three straight months of record ICE arrests — in August the agency said it arrested 50,925 people across the country, the highest number of "illegal aliens" arrested in a single month.

Between the lines: These arrests have been less conspicuous than high-profile raids that came early in the year, but impactful — called a "shadow surge" by one of the administration's opponents.

Zoom out: Immigration raids discourage legally authorized workers from reporting to job sites, Bill Owens, chairman of the National Association of Home Builders, recently said.

Higher mortgage rates and rising material costs are also weighing on the industry, he said.

Building material costs are up by a median 6.7% from last year, according to one NAHB survey.

The other side: "ICE is not arresting people legally in the country," said White House spokesperson Lauren Bis.

"There is no shortage of American minds and hands to grow our labor force."

The administration has said its new Office of Immigration Policy will help employers navigate immigration policies.

The big picture: Immigrants made up more than 26% of the construction workforce in 2024, the most recent Census Bureau data on the industry.

But in certain trades, the share is much higher — immigrants make up 57% of those working on drywall and 53% of roofers, according to an analysis of that data released earlier this year by NAHB.

description:

text:
AUSTIN (KXAN) — The Austin DoorDash delivery driver shot by federal immigration agents on Sunday remains in custody and says the bullet is still in his body, lodged near his spine.

28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garces Perez spoke by phone during a news conference Monday afternoon from the Pearsall Detention Facility. His attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, translated portions of his remarks, describing his physical condition and treatment following the shooting.

“He’s saying that he’s in a lot of pain, that they did not take out the bullet because it was close to his spine, but that they had him in a very cold room without a bed,” Wilber said during the phone call.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security confirmed Wilber was in federal custody pending removal from the country. In a statement, DHS said he entered the United States illegally.

However, U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, D-TX, said Wilber entered the country legally through the now-discontinued CBP One program. His attorney acknowledged that he later missed a court date, resulting in a removal order.

Wife says she struggled to find answers

Wilber’s wife, Elizdar, told their attorney that she wanted to spend Sunday with her husband, but he chose to work to earn money for the family.

According to Elizdar, she received a phone call from Wilber telling her he had been shot and was in pain, but she was given little information about where he was being treated. She said hospital security personnel told her her husband was not there.

Supporters at Monday’s news conference said the family’s experience has only added to the uncertainty surrounding the shooting and Wilber’s detention.

“This is about a wife and a mother that is suffering,” Casar said. “This is about a husband and a father who is in pain without pain medication in a prison in the desert right now.”

Questions surrounding the shooting

Lincoln-Goldfinch disputed the federal government’s account of the encounter and argued her client never attempted to evade officers.

“He asked the ICE officer if he could please at least pull over so that they could detain him,” she said. “They said no, and they side-swiped him basically. He did a U-turn to try and find a spot to park so that he could go with them. And they basically ran into him and then shot him.”

The attorney also said agents did not initially identify themselves through emergency equipment.

“So they never asked him to stop and never turned on any sort of police lights or siren,” she said. “The only time they turned on any lights or siren was after they side-swiped him and hit him.”

The circumstances leading up to the shooting remain under investigation.

Community leaders demand accountability

The news conference drew civil rights advocates, elected officials and community members who criticized federal immigration enforcement practices and called for greater transparency.

“What is happening is unacceptable,” said Gabriel Rosales, the Texas state director for LULAC.

Rosales later added, “We need to hold every ICE agent accountable and every elected official that voted to fund these people.”

Jeff Travillion, Travis County commissioner and local NAACP chair, questioned the tactics used by immigration agents.

“How does America get in the position of funding a secret police force who covers its face,” Travillion questioned.

Rev. Erin Walter, executive director of the Texas Unitarian Universalist Justice Ministry, warned that concerns surrounding immigration enforcement extend beyond immigrant communities.

“To my white siblings, you are just as much at risk right now with this terror in our communities as anyone,” Walter said.

National LULAC President Roman Palomares also condemned the incident.

“A federal badge is not a shield,” Palomares said. “A mask is not a license.”

Calls for body camera footage, independent investigation

Attorneys and elected officials used the news conference to push for several policy changes, including:

Release of body camera footage within 24 hours of critical incidents

An end to ICE-conducted traffic stops

Termination of 287(g) agreements that allow local law enforcement agencies to assist with federal immigration enforcement

They also called for an independent investigation into the shooting.

“Clearly ICE has no credibility anymore. It lies,” said U.S. Rep. Lloyd Doggett, D-TX.

Casar said the case raises concerns regardless of political affiliation.

“I don’t care if you’re Democrat or Republican,” Casar said. “We all believe the federal government should not be allowed to shoot you and then disappear you from the country so that no one can be held responsible.”

Attorney seeks release from detention

Lincoln-Goldfinch said her most immediate concern is securing medical treatment for her Wilber and removing him from detention while he recovers.

She said she has filed a temporary restraining order seeking his release from the Pearsall Detention Facility.

“We are fed up with ICE and DHS telling us lies about what has happened in these incidents where people are being murdered and shot,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

title: Federal judge questions ICE credibility in hearing on Oregon arrests - Statesman Journal

text:
A federal judge questioned the government's credibility after a deportation officer admitted his report on an arrest in Ashland was inaccurate.

Innovation Law Lab alleges the government is violating a court order that prohibits most warrantless immigration arrests in Oregon.

Four immigrants testified about being arrested or encountered by federal agents without a warrant.

PORTLAND — A federal deportation officer acknowledged under oath in federal court that his written report for the arrest of a man in Ashland was inaccurate, prompting U.S. District Court Judge Mustafa Kasubhai to question the federal government's credibility in documenting warrantless immigration arrests in Oregon.

"Right now your client (the federal government) doesn't have a lot of credibility when it comes to documentation," Kasubhai said during closing arguments Sept. 21, referencing the officer's testimony and other evidence heard during a two-day hearing.

The testimony and arguments came as lawyers for Innovation Law Lab claimed the federal government is “routinely, openly and brazenly” violating a preliminary injunction prohibiting warrantless immigration arrests in the state. The organization sued the Trump administration after Operation Black Rose began, a monthslong federal immigration enforcement campaign conducted by the Department of Homeland Security that started in late September 2025 and resulted in more than 1,500 arrests statewide.

Kasubhai on Feb. 4 granted a preliminary injunction barring U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement from conducting warrantless arrests in Oregon unless agents first determine that a specific person is likely to evade authorities before a warrant can be obtained.

The government has "not halted their illegal warrantless arrest policy and practice," wrote lawyers with Innovation Law Lab in a motion filed Sept. 4. “In fact, the Defendants have doubled down on their illegal policy or practice by issuing instructions to their agents that blatantly violate the Court’s injunction with respect to the subclass.”

They also cite data from the Portland Immigration Rights Council and the Deportation Data Project showing continued and growing arrest activity after the injunction. There were 109 arrests in January, 41 arrests in February, 30 in March, 64 in April, 83 in May, 186 in June and 174 in July.

The Trump administration arrested a record number of people across the U.S. in July.

Alyssa Walker Keller, co-executive director for PIRC, wrote in a declaration and testified in court that after “unprecedented” reported detentions in the fall and winter, there was a “sudden drop” in reports of detentions to the organization’s hotline in February 2026.

“While detentions were still happening there were less than five per week. This lasted for around two to three months. We believe that this was in large part due to the preliminary injunction issued by the District Court,” Walker Keller said.

The hotline has now experienced a “sustained increase” in calls since May, she said.

Walker Keller said most reports involve arrests after a traffic stop in the street, at a local courthouse, or in public parking lots.

The Ashland arrest was among four arrests described in testimony and declarations that lawyers said showed that federal agents have continued making arrests that violate the injunction. Lawyers said testimony from the government's witness, a deportation officer identified only as J.G., also confirmed the government has failed to follow the reporting ordered by Kasubhai in February.

Four immigrants in Oregon testify in court about ICE enounters

Innovation Law Lab's motion cites declarations from individuals who describe being boxed in by vehicles, handcuffed, searched and transported before federal agents even confirmed who they were.

The four individuals testified during an eight-hour evidentiary hearing on Sept. 18.

The witnesses included a Medford McDonald’s employee who filed a declaration saying he was boxed in by two vans around 4:05 a.m. on June 13 as he arrived for work. The man, identified only as CJVM, testified in federal court remotely, describing himself as a two-year resident of Medford with a wife and two daughters who first arrived in the country in May 2024 seeking political asylum.

CJVM, who said he no longer works for the restaurant, remembered five men and one woman surrounding his vehicle. He acknowledged reaching over to the passenger seat to try to reach his cellphone to record as officers began to shout. He estimated 30 seconds passed before agents broke the driver-side window.

CJVM said agents forcibly grabbed his arm and handcuffed him.

Agents took a picture of his face and eventually ran his information, discovering he had an active asylum application and was complying with release terms. CJVM said agents apologized and let him go. He also said the same cars kept showing up at the McDonald’s parking lot at the same time for about three consecutive weekends, prompting the manager to arrange transportation for employees to reduce risk when driving to work.

CJVM said in court that he was "still afraid" and had "kept the trauma of what happened that day."

Another man, identified only as HDGH, said he was arrested alongside a friend, MTM, after they were followed by ICE officers from a Walmart parking lot after buying supplies for a fishing trip on July 26.

The 22-year-old said in court he has lived in Medford since 2021, except for six months when he lived in California.

Agents followed the two for 30 minutes to Emigrant Lake, he recalled. HDGH said agents handcuffed both men and identified the men only after they were taken to the Medford ICE office.

HDGH said agents “tried to pressure” them to self-deport, offering money, but both refused. He described the agents as "angry" after he refused, when asked to describe why he felt pressured.

“When we got to Portland, they said they had to let us go and let us go a few blocks from the office. I understand that a federal judge ordered ICE to release us and that is the only reason we were released,” HDGH said in his declaration.

A Eugene resident, HFMJ, said he works as a landscaper to support three children. He and his roommate were traveling to work around 7:15 a.m. on July 3 when ICE vehicles began following their car. HFMJ said agents arrested his coworker and then approached the car.

“They told me to 'get out of the car, we’re arresting you. We have an arrest warrant.' But they never showed me any papers,” HFMJ said.

HFMJ said in court he was not asked his name or anything about his identity before being handcuffed. Agents did not pull their IDs or identify the two men until they were at the ICE office.

HFMJ also described being pressured to sign documentation he did not understand. Kasubhai questioned if officers explained he was being asked to sign a voluntary deportation order. HFMJ said they did not.

He was released, and now every Monday reports to ICE with an app on his cellphone as a condition of that release, HFMJ said.

And JCCV said he was arrested after leaving the parking lot of a Walmart in Hood River on June 19.

The 34-year-old has lived in The Dalles for a year and a half, according to his testimony.

JCCV said he has an ongoing asylum case. The man said he was also approved for Temporary Protected Status but no longer has TPS after the Trump administration terminated it for Venezuela. JCCV said his work authorization has not expired. JCCV said his wife and his children, a 10-year-old daughter and 14-year-old son, live with him in The Dalles.

JCCV, a delivery driver for Walmart through the Spark app and also a DoorDash and Instacart driver, remembered being cut off in the road as he returned to pick up another order.

JCCV said officers took his belongings and put his hands in handcuffs without asking for ID or showing any warrant.

He said agents took him to Cascade Locks, about 25 minutes away, before he was first questioned and asked his name. Agents then drove JCCV to Portland, where he waited for hours and was told to sign a paper.

JCCV said he was “intimidated” into signing and then taken to the Tacoma detention center. At Tacoma, JCCV said an officer gave him documents eight or 10 days into detention describing the arrest. It included false information, he said, claiming that he was in a Toyota Camry. He was driving a 2010 Toyota Corolla.

JCCV told the court that the owner of the car in the paperwork is his brother and that, after reviewing the paperwork, he believes he was mistakenly detained. He said his brother was at the same place for the same work at the same time.

JCCV has since been released from detention.

Deportation officer testifies in court and acknowledges authoring inaccurate report

The government called deportation officer JG as its witness. The deportation officer said he currently works out of the Medford office and said he's been with ICE for 11 months. He is a former Grants Pass police officer and former officer with the Department of Veterans' Affairs, according to his testimony.

He said he has 15 years of experience total as a law enforcement officer.

JG said he was physically present in the encounters involving HDGH and CJVM.

In the case of CJVM, JG said officers had run the license plate "a couple weeks" before the encounter. Their target, he said, had a final order for removal. CJVM was not that target, he acknowledged.

Agents had a photo of the target but said it was dark out and that CJVM placed a hand over his face, limiting agents when they attempted to identify the driver. He estimated CJVM was handcuffed for two minutes.

In the arrest of HDGH, JG testified that officers that morning were running license plates of cars in the Medford Walmart lot. They ran the plate of the car HDGH was in and discovered the registered owner, MTM, was reportedly in the country unlawfully.

Officers followed the vehicle to Emigrant Lake because ICE has instituted a policy barring vehicle stops. That policy came in the wake of two fatal ICE shootings in Maine and Houston.

In court, JG acknowledged he authored a report about the arrest that would make it seem as if he already knew who HDGH was prior to the encounter.

JG said he wrote the narrative for the driver and "pretty much" wrote it identical to the narrative for HDGH's arrest.

JG, reading the narrative, said he had written that the Medford office had initiated an investigation to locate and apprehend HDGH. That was not possible, he said.

"I did not even know he existed," JG said.

Judge also questions government claiming warrants perpetual

The judge also ordered supplemental briefs on Sept. 18, which were discussed Sept. 21, after Assistant U.S. Attorney Ariana N. Garousi argued that a 2023 warrant for JCCV was still valid. That 2023 warrant preceded an eight-day detention when he first arrived in the United States.

The judge said when someone is released from custody it "generally means" a warrant is resolved. If someone is wanted back in custody, would another warrant not then have to be issued, he asked?

Garouisi argued that yes, a previous warrant in an immigrant's file, even if it has already been executed, can be used for future arrests. Garouisi cited a federal law that reads the Attorney General may, at any time, revoke a bond or parole, rearrest the alien under the original warrant, and detain the alien.

Kasubhai said the precondition is a revocation of a bond or parole. He questioned where in the evidence it showed JCCV's bond or parole was revoked.

Jordan Cunnings with Innovation Law Lab described the argument as "pretty astonishing."

"The government is making a pretty astonishing argument that once they have probable cause to arrest someone, even if they've later determined that person is not a flight risk or a danger to the community and can live at peace while their immigration proceedings are ongoing, that initial warrant can be used again at any time to detain someone for any reason or for no reason at all," she said. "The law doesn't support that, nor does the Constitution."

Innovation Law Lab asks court for more reporting as relief

Innovation Law Lab is asking Kasubhai to enforce the injunction against the federal government to protect other immigrants in Oregon who they say are being harmed every day.

They said the administration is failing to fully comply with the injunction's reporting requirements, which required a report of the facts and circumstances surrounding warrantless immigration arrests conducted in Oregon every 30 days.

Of the more than 500 arrests in Oregon since February, the government has reported about 25 as warrantless, according to its testimony.

Innovation Law Lab's motion argues that ICE has not consistently provided the required documentation for warrantless arrests and has not produced complete records when plaintiffs requested information on April 20, May 18, July 10, and Aug. 21 regarding specific civil immigration arrests they believed were warrantless.

Cunnings said Innovation Law Lab was happy to see "the depth of the unreliability of the documents" the government is producing and "falsification of information" come to light.

"We're confident that the judge is going to make a good decision that restores the validity of the force of his injunction, preventing warrantless arrests in Oregon," Cunnings said.

Innovation Law Lab said the government is violating the order in two ways, repeatedly conducting warrantless arrests and failing to document and report them. They are asking the court to order the government to provide all documents related to warrantless arrests, including body camera footage.

JG said Oregon deportation officers received body cameras about a month ago.

On Sept. 4, the judge ordered U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to turn over discovery about warrantless arrests in Oregon ahead of the Sept. 18 hearing, and ordered the administration to produce any document redacted or withheld in unredacted form within 7 days of the order.

He also ordered the names, contact information and narrative descriptions of events of any noncitizens in documents related to events that took place Oct. 29 through Oct. 31, 2025, when one of the plaintiffs, M-J-M-A, was arrested in Woodburn, as well as the names of any agents, from documents related to that same period.

On Sept. 21, Kasubhai ordered additional supplemental briefs be filed within seven days and said he would work on issuing his order.

text:
One of the nation's largest Hispanic civil rights groups called Monday for the Venezuelan illegal immigrant who was shot during an ICE pursuit in Austin to not be deported, arguing he is a key witness in the investigation into officers' use of force.

The League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC) made the statements Monday afternoon after an agent shot and wounded Wilber Rafael Garces Perez during a traffic stop. Garces Perez was hospitalized in serious but stable condition. The shooting sparked protests in Austin and calls from local officials for an independent investigation.

"Wilber is a victim of the shooting and the most important witness to it. You do not deport the key witness to your own officers' use of force," LULAC CEO Juan Peruano said.

According to Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, the attorney for Garces Perez and his wife, Garces Perez was delivering DoorDash when an "unmarked black truck sideswiped him."

ICE SHOOTING ROCKS AUSTIN AS DEMOCRAT DEMANDS BODYCAM VIDEO, INDEPENDENT PROBE

She said he did not know the vehicle was operated by ICE and subsequently made a U-turn under the highway before the agents continued to pursue him.

"The truck chased him and sideswiped him again. And the agents came out and shot him in the back of the neck and pulled him out of the car," Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

Lincoln-Goldfinch also claimed Garces Perez did not receive sufficient medical care, and the bullet remained lodged hours after the shooting.

ICE OFFICER PLEADS NOT GUILTY TO LYING ABOUT MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING INVOLVING VENEZUELAN MAN

"We learned that at 4:00 he still had a bullet lodged in his back. He was shot here in his back, and they didn't take the bullet out, and they didn't give him pain medication. And they transferred him to ICE, to a processing center, where he spent the night without a bed," Lincoln-Goldfinch said. "There is absolutely zero justification for having shot him in the back of the neck. And this is why we're calling for a stop to ICE traffic stops. ICE officers are over armed, overpaid, under trained and violent. They don't know how to safely conduct traffic stops."

According to his attorney, Garces Perez had a work permit and was seeking asylum after entering the U.S. in 2024 through the CBP One app, which the Biden administration expanded to allow migrants to request asylum at ports of entry.

His attorney claimed he received a removal order after a notice for his immigration hearing was sent to his old address, despite him having updated his address with the court.

"He changed his address with the immigration court, and a notice of hearing was sent to his old address. He didn't know he had a hearing. He didn't go. And so he got a deportation order in absentia, which is a very common thing," she said. "The court is notorious for sending notices of hearings to the wrong address. So it appears that that is what happened with him. That's why he has a removal order. We are working on that."

According to the Austin Police Department, hundreds of protesters gathered Sunday evening following the ICE operation, throwing rocks, bottles and pieces of concrete. Three police vehicles were damaged, and multiple officers sustained minor injuries, officials said.

At least three people were arrested for rioting, resisting arrest, assaulting a peace officer, or a combination of the charges. The individuals were identified as Robert Padgett, 48; Armando Menagarcia, 29; and Matthew Hemby, 44.

Lincoln-Goldfinch further to condemned the accounts provided by federal agents, claiming ICE officials do not tell the truth.

"We are fed up with ICE and DHS telling us lies about what has happened in these incidents where people are being murdered and shot," she said.

Rep. Lloyd Doggett echoed Lincoln-Goldfinch's assertions, claiming that federal immigration officials often lie.

"ICE has no credibility anymore. It lies. We know it lies. We've seen it demonstrated again and again, and we need the kind of independent structure to demand some accountability," he said.

DHS sources confirmed to Fox News on Sunday that Garces Perez is an illegal immigrant from Venezuela with a final order of removal.

DHS said Garces Perez illegally entered the United States under the Biden administration. The agency said he was shot during a law enforcement operation.

text:
When a mother returned to Maryland earlier this year after four months in Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention, her children, ages one and four, did not recognize her at first. In her absence, they had lived with Vidal Rivas, an Episcopal priest who had agreed to be their temporary guardian if immigration authorities took her into custody.

The experience was demanding. But Rivas, 62, stands ready to do the same for 29 other children whose immigrant parents have named him as their standby guardian. Two more families are making similar arrangements with him, he says.

Inside the church hangs a sign bearing the same message in English, Spanish and Haitian Creole: “We love migrants.” For Rivas, the words have become a commitment to the families who fear an immigration arrest could suddenly separate them from their children.

Rivas began encouraging families to name him as a standby guardian last year, shortly after President Donald Trump returned to office. Nearly all of the parents are Salvadoran, like him, and have been bracing for the Trump Administration to end Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, for roughly 170,000 immigrants from that country.

Under Maryland law, parents can designate a standby guardian in the event they are arrested by immigration authorities. The designated guardian automatically becomes the child’s legal guardian for six months, with the possibility to extend if approved by a judge. Rivas says some parents have talked to him about contingency plans in case they remain in a detention center for longer.

Maryland was among the first states to revise its guardianship laws to help prevent the children of detained immigrants from entering foster care. During Trump’s first term, state lawmakers passed a law allowing families to name a temporary guardian if detention or deportation separates their family. In July, Massachusetts made a similar change in state law, joining Virginia, New York, California, Nevada, and Washington, D.C. to streamline such arrangements.

After the mother of two young children was released, Rivas and his wife remained close to the family. “We now feel like the children's grandparents, because we still have a close relationship with her, looking after her and looking after the children,” he says.

Caring for the two children made Rivas acutely aware of the scale of what he has agreed to. If immigration enforcement ramps up in Hyattsville, a small city where more than a third of the population is Hispanic, he could be called upon to care for many children at once

Such fears have been further exacerbated by the uncertainty surrounding TPS, a program Congress created in 1990 to protect immigrants who cannot safely return to countries affected by armed conflict, natural disasters, or other extraordinary conditions. El Salvador was the first country designated for TPS in 1990 due to its civil war, and that protection was renewed in 2001 after the country. Since 1990, more than 170,000 Salvadorans have been granted TPS status, becoming one of the largest groups protected by the program.

In early September, hours before the TPS designation for Salvadorans was set to expire, the Department of Homeland Security released a notice that suggested it would remain in place for now. The short notice said Salvadorans under TPS would continue to “retain protection including work authorization,” but added that an announcement on the program’s future “will be made at the appropriate time.”

Maryland is home to many Salvadorans who fled to the United States in the 1990s or the early 2000s. Around that time, El Salvador was just rebuilding itself from a brutal civil war, before a powerful hurricane and a pair of earthquakes hit the Central American country.

For those who have been in the United States for more than 20 years, returning home may no longer feel like a viable option. More than 27% of El Salvaror’s population lives below the national poverty line, according to the World Bank. It also has the highest imprisonment rate in the world, according to data from the World Prison Brief, a database compiled by the Institute for Crime & Justice Policy Research (ICPR) at Birkbeck, University of London. President Nayib Bukele has overseen an aggressive crackdown on gang violence as well as critics of his administration. The strategy is credited with reducing the country’s crime rate, but rights groups accuse his government of arbitrary detention and abuses in prison. Last year, Trump sent hundreds of deported Venezuelan migrants to El Salvador’s CECOT, a maximum security jail designated for gang members.

Rivas came to the U.S. in 1998 to work at a Catholic Church in Washington, D.C., where his advocacy work put him at odds with the church’s leadership. He eventually converted to the more liberal Episcopalian Church, and joined St. Matthews in 2008.

As the church’s Hispanic membership has grown, Rivas has felt an increasing responsibility to help parishioners struggling with immigration issues. Watching parents cry as they discussed what might happen to them—and their children—convinced him that he had to do more.

text:
The government has reiterated that its management of foreign nationals entering or staying in the country strictly aligns with the Constitution, national laws, and international treaties.

The Ministry of International Relations and Trade issued the statement Tuesday in response to a 2 September report by Amnesty International concerning Angolan women and children displaced by severe drought who have crossed into Namibia.

Reaffirming its position, the Ministry emphasized that Namibia remains fully committed to protecting human rights, safeguarding women and children, keeping families together, and providing access to basic essential services for anyone within its borders.

“The movement of persons across the Namibia—Angola border is a matter of mutual interest and concern, which requires close cooperation and coordination between our two countries,” they noted, adding that the government remains fully committed to pursuing a lawful, humane, durable and dignified approach to the situation of suspected Angolan women and children wandering the streets of towns in Namibia.

According to the ministry, the matter continues to be dealt with in consultation with Angola and other relevant stakeholders, consistent with the principles of sovereignty, good neighbourliness, regional cooperation and the longstanding bonds of friendship and solidarity between Namibia and Angola.

“Namibia further notes, taking into consideration the need for constructive engagement in matters of this nature, that the report by Amnesty International was published without adequate prior consultation with the Namibian Government or sufficient time for the government to provide relevant information, clarification and its views on the matters addressed in the report,” highlighted the Ministry.

Reiterating the government’s position, the Ministry reaffirmed its willingness to engage openly and constructively with all relevant stakeholders with a view to ensuring that matters concerning international migration are addressed in a manner consistent with applicable national laws and Namibia’s international obligations, as well as the principles of humanity, dignity, security and regional cooperation.

text:
Wilber Rafael Garces Perez came to Austin two years ago, seeking asylum.

The 28-year-old Venezuelan immigrant delivered meals for DoorDash to support his family, putting his earnings toward medical care for his son, who has a disability, his lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said in a Monday post on Instagram.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

On Sunday afternoon, a masked Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shot and wounded Garces Perez in an incident that has roiled the city during a national surge in federal immigration enforcement and deportations.

“This is about a family,” U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Austin, said at a Monday press conference. “What kind of America do we want to be?”

Before he was thrust into national news, Garces Perez was a husband, father and son. He grew up in Yaritagua, Venezuela — known as “Sugar City” for its sweet cane production. His hometown was reported by two Venezuelan news outlets and confirmed on Tuesday by Fabiana Meléndez Ruiz, a spokesperson working with the Venezuelan man’s family.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Flor Pérez described her son as a hard worker and a calm, friendly and kind person. She said in an interview that he was the sole provider for herself and his son, who lives with her in Venezuela.

“He’s never had problems before, not even in high school, they never complained about him,” she said in Spanish. “Everyone loves him.”

After attending a local high school, Garces Perez studied banking and finance at a technical and engineering school, the Instituto Universitario de Tecnología de Yaracu, Meléndez Ruiz confirmed. He entered the United States legally in 2024 seeking asylum and obtained a work permit, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

“He emigrated to the US because he wanted to give me a better life,” Pérez said. “He wanted to go there to see if he could find better opportunities to be able to take care of us and achieve his dreams.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Because of a change of address, he missed a hearing notice in his immigration proceedings, and the federal government ordered him deported in a final order of removal. Lincoln-Goldfinch said Garces Perez has no criminal record.

In a statement late Sunday, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said that Garces Perez had a final order of removal and that he had entered the country without legal status. ICE did not respond to questions seeking more information about the man’s criminal record or his immigration status.

Loved ones recount day of ICE shooting

On Sunday morning, Garces Perez’s wife, Elizdar, asked her husband to stay home and spend the day with her. But he left to pick up some DoorDash orders, driving through North Austin to deliver meals, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. Elizdar declined to speak to the media.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Around 12:40 p.m. Austin time, Garces Perez’s mother received a video call from her son.

He said “Mom, immigration is following me. They shot me,” Pérez told a Venezuelan digital news outlet in an interview conducted in Spanish. He was screaming loudly and quickly hung up to call his wife, she said.

He then called Elizdar. When the call was disconnected suddenly, she drove to the highway underpass where he had been. There, she found his sedan with the passenger side crushed.

Garces Perez said a masked ICE agent in a black SUV drove aggressively next to his blue sedan. The agent did not turn on sirens or lights until after the car hit his passenger side as he was trying to make a U-turn and park, Garces Perez told the media on Monday. He gave his account of what happened over the phone from where he is currently being detained in Pearsall.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

When stopped in the 8000 block of Anderson Lane, the agent shot through the passenger window, striking Garces Perez in the back, below his neck.

“There is absolutely zero justification for having shot him in the back of the neck,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said. ICE did not respond to questions about why force was used.

For hours on Sunday afternoon, Elizdar waited anxiously across the street from Dell Seton Hospital in downtown Austin, where city officials had said her husband was getting medical care. Dressed in a light blue shirt and pants, she held her head as Lincoln-Goldfinch demanded answers from police, who would not let them inside the hospital nor answer questions about his condition.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

After Mayor Kirk Watson urged the hospital to contact the family, they were told around 6 p.m. that he had been moved and taken into ICE custody, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. He had been given one pill for pain at the hospital, the lawyer added.

Overnight, Elizdar slept with her phone under her pillow, waiting for an update about her husband’s condition and location. News wouldn’t come until more than 20 hours after the shooting occurred, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

At 10 a.m. on Monday, Elizdar and Lincoln-Goldfinch discovered Garces Perez was being held in federal custody at the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, roughly 135 miles southwest of Austin.

Garces Perez spoke by phone to reporters on Monday afternoon, saying that he had not received pain medication while detained. He said he is in a lot of pain because of the bullet lodged in his back, which doctors said they could not remove because it was too close to his spine.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

He also said he did not receive proper wound dressing. Dell Seton representatives did not respond to a request for comment.

Pérez said she believes her son eventually wants to move back to Venezuela to be with his family, who relies on him for support. Pérez had a knee surgery three weeks ago, but without her son’s income, she cannot begin therapy.

She said she is grateful for the support her son has received and asked the community to keep supporting immigrants.

text:

(OSV News) — After a man was shot and wounded by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer in Austin, Texas, on Sept. 20, Bishop Daniel E. Garcia denounced the shooting and called for “a viable immigration policy that respects the rule of law while recognizing the dignity of every person.”

The individual who was shot was delivering for DoorDash at the time of the encounter with ICE, his lawyer said. A video obtained by CNN showed officers cutting off the man’s shirt after the incident, revealing a bullet wound in his back.

Bishop ‘saddened and disturbed’ by ICE shooting

In a Sept. 20 statement, Bishop Garcia, who leads the Diocese of Austin, said he was “deeply saddened and disturbed” by the shooting.

“We find ourselves in a time in this country and city, when people are living in terror and fear because of the increased activity of ICE agents on our streets. Many people are often being detained only due to the color of their skin or the language they speak,” he said. “Today the credibility of a federal agency that is supposed to protect us has been weakened by incidences such as the one that took place today.

“I ask the faithful of the Diocese of Austin to pray for this man who was shot, his family, for all those who have been affected, all who have been involved and for our entire community,” Bishop Garcia continued. “As an investigation begins, let us pray that the Federal, State and City authorities will be transparent and honest about what occurred this afternoon, so that confidence in our governmental entities may be strengthened, not weakened.”

Austin city officials have called for an independent investigation of the incident.

Legal status disputed of victim in ICE shooting

In a statement posted on X, the Department of Homeland Security said, “Homeland Security Investigations, with the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, is leading the investigation into the officer involved shooting of an illegal alien from Venezuela, who illegally entered our country under the Biden administration and had a final order of removal, during a law enforcement operation today in Austin, TX.”

“The illegal alien’s condition is stable, and he is in federal custody pending removal,” the statement said. “This is a developing situation, and we will update the public when more information becomes available.”

But Austin immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch said in a series of posts on X that she is representing the man, whom she identified as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28. Lincoln-Goldfinch contested the government’s characterization, saying Perez was a “legal immigrant.” She said he lawfully entered the United States through the CBP One program for asylum seekers — the program was discontinued in 2025 — and has a valid work permit.

“The issue regarding the deportation order is that he moved and changed addresses. There was a notice for a hearing sent to the wrong address that he missed, which is VERY common. We are working on that,” she said. “He will be released from detention, his immigration matter will be resolved, and the agencies will be held accountable.”

Bishop: Human dignity does not depend on citizenship

Bishop Garcia added in his statement, “We need not forget that regardless of a person’s immigration status, every person is created in the image and likeness of God and possesses an inherent dignity that must always be respected and protected. May God assist us in finding resolve and peace during these troubling times.”

“We are reminded, during this National Migrant Week, of an essential truth of our faith: we are all brothers and sisters,” he continued. “When one person is harmed, all of us are affected. We cannot allow differences of citizenship to diminish our recognition of the dignity that belongs to every human being.”
