text:
A Haitian pastor who went from being stopped for a broken taillight to being placed on a deportation flight to Haiti, only to be pulled off the plane at the last minute, has had his bid to remain in the United States denied, his former employer said Monday.

The Department of Homeland Security has denied Molis Augustave’s pending application for lawful permanent residency in the U.S., said We Are CASA, a national immigrant rights group where he previously worked.

Augustave had a pending immigration application to adjust his status when police in York, Pennsylvania, stopped him on Sept. 4 while he was making food deliveries for DoorDash. The next day, he was turned over to Immigration and Customs Enforcement, We Are CASA said.

Days after his arrest, his wife, Omara Boniface Nunez, a U.S. citizen, received word from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services that a petition she had filed on behalf of a relative had been approved. Augustave had separately applied to adjust his status to become a permanent resident.

But on Sept. 17, he was awakened early and told to prepare to leave. He was already aboard an ICE charter flight when, he said, “at the last minute, they pulled me off. They were going to unjustly deport me to Haiti,” Augustave said in a statement provided by We Are CASA.

Facing deportation

Augustave worked as an organizer for the group before his Temporary Protected Status expired in July, along with protections for more than 300,000 other Haitians in the United States. The termination has left many Haitians vulnerable to deportation.

Among them is Sirena Prosper, a longtime Pompano Beach community member and business owner who is the mother of seven children who are U.S. citizens, three of them minors. Prosper, who was born in The Bahamas but has lived in the U.S. since she was six months old, is in ICE custody and faces deportation to Haiti, say faith organizers who announced a 6:30 p.m. Tuesday candlelight vigil at Royal Hands Salon, 230 S. Cypress Rd., Suite 1, in Pompano, to demand her release and an end to family separation.

Similar calls are also being made on behalf of Augustave, who remains in ICE custody even though he was not ultimately among the 89 people deported to the Caribbean country last week. He said he was being held with more than 100 other detainees.

“I have met men who are scared, men who cry, and men who have no idea what is going to happen to them,” Augustave said. “One man told me he wanted to die. I sat with him and talked to him about God. Then I saw him smile again.

“My life is not worth more because I am a pastor. My family does not matter more than others because people heard our story,” he added. “I am asking people to also see the others who were on that plane and the people still behind these walls.”

Homeland Security did not respond to a request for comment about Augustave’s case. A motion to reopen his removal proceedings remains pending before the Board of Immigration Appeals. A habeas corpus petition challenging his detention also remains pending before the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Louisiana. Though he remains in ICE custody, advocates say they are concerned the government will again attempt to deport him to Haiti as early as this week.

“We called on the government to give Pastor Molis the fair and thorough review that is required under the law. They did the opposite,” said Ama Frimpong, chief of services and legal advocacy at We Are CASA. “We secured time, but time on its own is not justice. USCIS, which has simply become a force multiplier for ICE, rushed this application and denied it prematurely. We must hold USCIS accountable to its duties. We demand that USCIS reconsider and reverse this unjust decision.”

The group said it’s calling for Augustave’s release and reunification with his wife and two children while his immigration proceedings continue, and for his various requests for immigration relief to be fairly adjudicated on the merits.

Augustave came to the U.S. in 2016 and his request for political asylum was denied two years later. After an appeal was also denied, and he was issued a final order of removal, he received protection under TPS, the humanitarian program that allows nationals of countries facing armed conflict, natural disasters or extraordinary conditions to temporarily live and work legally in the United States.

The Trump administration moved last year to terminate Haiti’s TPS designation, a decision that was challenged in federal court. The administration subsequently asked the Supreme Court to allow the termination to take effect while litigation continues.

In June, the court granted the request, which has meant that those once protected returned to the status they had before — which the administration has been using to detain people and deny their requests for adjustment of status.

Human Rights Watch issues plea

Since last month, Homeland Security has increased deportation flights to Haiti from monthly to weekly, and returned more than 450 individuals to Cap-Haïtien, on the country’s northern coast.

The city has become the principal arrival point of entry for flights because armed gangs have made the airport in Port-au-Prince unsafe. As Haitians flee the violence, the northern city has seen its population triple, Human Rights Watch said Monday, sounding the alarm over the pressure U.S. deportations are placing on Haiti.

The organization warned that Haitians returning from the U.S., face threats to their lives and receive little to no support. It called on the U.S. Senate to urgently pass House-approved legislation that would reinstate TPS for Haitians.

Many of those deported had lived in the U.S. for years and were separated from family members who are U.S. citizens, Human Rights Watch said. Others had pending asylum claims. Haitian government officials told the organization that they lack funding, staff and the policy framework to safely receive and assist deportees.

“The United States is returning people, some with pending asylum claims, to a country that doesn’t have the capacity to protect them from violence, let alone help them find food and shelter,” Nathalye Cotrino, senior Americas researcher at Human Rights Watch, said. “The U.S. government should immediately halt these removals.”

Human Rights Watch said its researchers visited Cap-Haïtien from Aug. 24-30, and interviewed 44 Haitian deportees who had arrived on the first two deportation flights following the end of TPS. They also spoke to Haitian government officials and international officials involved in receiving them.

Researchers were also at the airport on Aug, 27 where they documented the arrival of a deportation flight and saw the reception firsthand.

Most people interviewed said they originally fled Haiti because of the country’s longstanding security and humanitarian crises, which have only worsened over the years. Some left after the 2010 earthquake, but the vast majority left after the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moïse and the deepening violence and instability that followed.

Most said that ICE had detained them before TPS formally ended and never explained the basis for their detention. Most said that while protected by TPS they had also filed asylum claims. Some said their claims were still pending at the time of their removal, and that they were unable to contact their lawyers or appear before an immigration judge before being deported.

Beyond limited assistance in urgent cases, Haitian authorities and humanitarian agencies do not offer sustained shelter, health care, transportation, protection or reintegration support. After being registered upon arrival, many deportees were left to fend for themselves, and did not know what to do or where to go next.

Some returned to their hometowns, but because of the security situation, many instead tried to reach relatives or friends elsewhere in the country, traveling the same day or remaining in Cap-Haïtien for days while waiting for money transfers to make the trip.

Many had lived in the U.S. for years, residing in Florida, New York, Indiana, Massachusetts, Ohio, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania. Interviewees had worked in construction, health care, manufacturing, hospitality, logistics, retail or agriculture.

Rushed decision

Augustave and his wife have been married since March 2023. They have a 2-year-old son, Isaac. Augustave is also a stepfather to Nunez’s 9-year-old daughter, Sofia.

Since Augustave’s detention, faith leaders have prayed and organized, alongside Haitian leaders and community organizations.

“People across the country called, shared his story, prayed, organized, and demanded that his case receive attention,” We Are CASA said.

The organization criticized DHS’s decision denying his green card application.

“Now DHS has shut the door on the process that should have decided his future,” the group said. “Rather than examine the complete record, evaluate his eligibility under the law, and reach a reasoned decision on the merits, the agency rushed to deny his application in an attempt to put him on the next deportation flight to Haiti.”

On Monday, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani raised the issue of TPS with President Trump, who is in the city for this year’s United Nations General Assembly, which he is scheduled to address on Tuesday.

Trump has revoked TPS for about a dozen countries including Haiti. New York state is home to an estimated 40,000 Haitians who had TPS.

Mamdani said he shared his “very strong opinions” with the president about how important “Haitian New Yorkers are not only to the fabric of our city but also to our city’s economy, to so many of the industries that build our city, and the stability that is in the president’s hands. And I appreciate the conversation that we had.”

text:
Federal immigration officials in Texas prevented US representative Veronica Escobar from fully conducting her congressional oversight duties at a controversial Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center, the lawmaker said in an interview with the Guardian.

Escobar, a Democrat who represents El Paso and surrounding areas on the US-Mexico border in west Texas, conducted an oversight visit last month at the Camp East Montana ICE tent facility housed in the Fort Bliss military base, after two separate “disturbances” had been reported there in recent weeks.

But when she arrived to scrutinize conditions at the camp, the largest ICE detention center in the country, she said she was not allowed to speak with any of the detained immigrants. She also requested surveillance footage of the reported incidents but said she has not received it.

“The administration obviously has attempted to block congressional oversight,” Escobar said in a telephone interview with the Guardian. “It’s been very challenging at times. And that has depended on, to a large extent, what the directive has been from the administration.”

The constraints placed on Escobar is one of the latest instances in which the Trump administration has limited members of Congress’s ability to conduct oversight visits into federal immigration detention centers.

Escobar and other federal lawmakers sued the Trump administration last year for blocking such access. Despite a federal judge ruling in favor of the lawmakers last December, there have been subsequent reports of ICE officials placing limits on or turning away members of congress when attempting to conduct oversight visits.

“Oversight, during the second Trump administration, has certainly been significantly more challenging than during the first Trump administration,” Escobar added.

Camp East Montana was hastily constructed last summer at the huge army base in El Paso. Unlike other ICE detention centers housed in buildings, this facility is a sprawling “soft-sided” tent camp. It has the capacity to hold up to 5,000 people and has drawn complaints and demands for its closure from the time it opened.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, reported two separate “disturbances” within one week there in early September. On 1 September, it alleged that detained immigrants assaulted security staff by striking, kicking and throwing tablets at them.

On 7 September, a larger group of around 130 detained immigrants allegedly threw items, flipped furniture and disabled security cameras. The detainees also knocked down partitions between the tented living quarters, known as pods, at the detention camp, Escobar said.

An ICE official at the facility called 911 during the incident, according to reporting by the El Paso Times. The newspaper’s revelation contradicted what ICE officials apparently told Escobar during her visit.

“While there absolutely have been serious issues and mismanagement, fraud, deaths, and a homicide, there had never been a riot,” Escobar said. “There had never been, especially in two weeks in a row, situations where the contractor lost control of the population in their custody.”

Escobar said that when she spoke with an ICE official about incidents, the official pointed to the detained immigrants’ nationality as the cause.

“The deputy was very quick to blame the nationality of the detainees, saying that the Venezuelans are a difficult population,” Escobar said.

It is still unclear what exactly happened during the two incidents.

Members of Congress have the legal power to conduct oversight visits into ICE detention facilities nationwide, by visiting the sites without prior notice and speaking with detained immigrants. Lawmakers have claimed that the Trump administration has limited those oversight visits by requiring lawmakers to submit the names and personal information of detainees they want to speak with beforehand.

The homeland security department disputed Escobar’s claims in an email to the Guardian, while adding that it considers many oversight visits “a media act”, and also denied that there has been an official request for data and footage.

“Any member of Congress can still request to speak with any illegal alien in ICE custody,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement. “If an illegal alien and a member of Congress agree to meet with one another, ICE will facilitate the meeting. We are not stopping members of Congress from meeting with illegal aliens, including many with criminal histories in ICE custody, or touring ICE facilities.”

Since Camp East Montana opened last summer, it has been plagued with accusations of abuse, mismanagement and dire conditions. Immigrants and human rights groups have repeatedly alleged human rights and constitutional violations at the site, including physical abuse, sexual harassment, inedible food and medical neglect. ICE was sued over alleged “dire” conditions earlier this year.

At least three people detained at the site have died in ICE custody, including a 55-year-old man whose January death was ruled a homicide after security guards beat him.

This year, an internal ICE inspection found a number of deficiencies at the site, including with guards’ use of force. A US government accountability office report also found a series of problems with the facility’s contract, its construction and the conditions. The office made four recommendations to DHS, ICE and the US army. Those recommendations remain “open”, meaning they have not been resolved.

“That facility, from my perspective, should not be operational,” Escobar said. “It should have been shut down a long time ago.”

During her recent Camp East Montana oversight visit, Escobar pressed for the private contractor running the facility to be held accountable for the recent incidents, not just the detained immigrants deemed responsible. Earlier this year, ICE gave the multi-million-dollar contract for running the facility on its behalf to a new private security company.

“The contractor needs to eat those costs [of the damage]. If they were not prepared, if they were unable to control the situation, the American taxpayer should not pay for their incompetence,” Escobar said. “These private contractors are making enormous sums of money. And frankly, there needed to be accountability with this contractor.”

The DHS spokesman said that far from closing, Camp East Montana “is upgrading” and claimed that the contractor now running the site was providing more services and “precise quality assurance”.

“ICE is always looking at ways to improve our detention facilities to ensure we are providing the best care to illegal aliens in our custody,” the spokesperson said.

Amentum Services, a Maryland-based contractor now running the Camp East Montana facility, did not respond to a request for comment.

Acquisition Logistics, a small and relatively-unknown company based in Virginia first secured a nearly $1.3bn contract to run the site. Amentum took over this April after previously working as a subcontractor at the site.

Meanwhile, there have been further accusations of alleged rights violations at other detention facilities. The Guardian has reported exclusively on a series of force feedings in ICE facilities, including inside two detention centers in Texas.

During the first Trump administration, Escobar criticized and investigated ICE’s use of force feeding on hunger strikers in 2019.

text:
President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 with a signature promise: the largest mass deportation effort by the federal government in U.S. history.

He said his administration would target the “worst of the worst,” hunting down and deporting immigrants with violent criminal histories.

But in reality, according to federal government data, under Trump, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportation officers — often aided by local police — have mostly arrested people with no criminal convictions.

The Texas Tribune interviewed five Texas immigrants — from Mexico, China, Iran, Cuba and Venezuela — who shared their experiences of being arrested by ICE and living in detention centers across the state.

Some entered the country legally only to see the rules change, while others were in the process of legalizing their immigration status. None have criminal convictions, according to immigration, state and federal court records. All are facing deportation.

Only 31% of the more than half million people arrested by ICE nationally as of Aug. 6 had a conviction. In Texas, where a quarter of all arrests happen, two of every three people ICE arrests have no criminal conviction.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in a statement the Trump administration will utilize “all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history, just as President Trump promised.” It added that ICE agents are targeting anyone in the country the Trump administration has classified as “illegal immigrants” — including immigrants the Biden administration allowed to legally enter.

Among the thousands now in Texas detention centers are spouses to U.S. citizens, including members of the military; immigrants who entered the country legally and then applied for permanent residency; college students who entered on student visas; and others who have lived in the country with the government’s blessing for decades under Temporary Protected Status before the Trump administration scrapped the program for selective countries.

Many have agreed to speedy deportations to escape detention centers that have been plagued by complaints about bad water, expired food and a lack of medical care. Others have fought, enduring detention for weeks or months in hopes that a judge will let them stay.

“Being in detention is a choice,” the DHS statement, encouraging people to self-deport. “If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return.”

Malena Chacón Santos, 24, Cuba

She came in legally, requested asylum and married a citizen. She’s been detained for 10 months.

By Alejandra Martinez

Around 8 a.m. on a November morning last year, Malena Chacón Santos walked into an Immigration and Customs Enforcement check-in in Dallas expecting to leave the same way she came in — with her husband waiting for her outside.

This was just a procedural appointment, nothing to fear, she thought.

Instead, she was detained.

Chacón Santos, a 24-year-old Cuban, had brought documents she believed showed she had followed the immigration process and had a right to live in the U.S. She tried to explain that to the officers with a shaky voice and staccato sentences.

But they would not look at her paperwork, she said. Instead, they told her to tell her family she would not be coming home.

She immediately called Juan Carlos Alvarez, the man she’d married nine months earlier.

“What is happening?” he asked.

Neither of them knew.

The next day, Chacón Santos was transferred more than 175 miles from her home to the Bluebonnet Detention Center in Anson, where she has spent nearly 10 months waiting for an answer about her future.

She came to the United States in November 2024 after spending about six months in Mexico waiting for an appointment to request asylum through CBP One cellphone app.

Chacón Santos said she did not want to cross the border illegally. She received her appointment and was allowed to enter the country on parole while her asylum claim was pending.

After living in communist Cuba, coming to the United States felt like a fresh start.

“Mi vida cambió,” she said quietly in Spanish. “My life changed.”

Her new life eventually brought her to Alvarez, an American citizen who served in the U.S. Army for two years. Chacón Santos, who is timid and soft spoken, said they met through a friend, began dating and developed what she described as “un sentimiento muy bonito de amor” — a beautiful feeling of love.

They married in February 2025.

Chacón Santos said she became a wife — and a stepmother to Alvarez’s three children. The family went to boxing classes, sporting events and visited museums. Chacón Santos and Alvarez loved reading books about personal growth and becoming better versions of themselves.

They had goals for their future. Maybe open a real estate business or a gym together.

Now, she draws superheroes and Disney princesses for her kids from her detention cell and writes love letters to Alvarez, telling him that he is always in her thoughts.

Alvarez calls her every day at 2 p.m. and 5 p.m. They whisper words of encouragement.

“Mi amor,” my love, Alvarez says.

“Mi rey,” my king, she replies.

“Todo va estar bien,” Everything is going to be OK, he assures her.

Every Sunday, Alvarez makes the three-hour drive to the detention center to see her.

He says Chacón Santos has been one of his strongest sources of support as a veteran with disability, including depression, anxiety and arthritis. She has accompanied him to medical appointments. Her absence has left a space in their family that cannot be filled.

“When this happened, it hurt us,” he said.

Chacón Santos says she can’t get used to the stiff detention bed or the bad food.

But detention has taught her to be strong. Reading and exercise help her stay calm, even as she worries about being deported.

And she still has faith that soon she will be beside her husband, continuing the life they had started building together.

Neither of them is giving up.

“We’ve done everything right,” he said. “Something has to give.”

Dixuan “Kai” Li, 27, China

After fleeing China to escape persecution of Christians, “I’m scared to be deported.”

By Uriel J. García

On the morning of May 20, Dixuan “Kai” Li was leaving her Arlington apartment with her husband for the gym when two U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers approached them.

After they confirmed the 27-year-old Li’s identity, the officers escorted her into an unmarked Ford truck and whisked her way.

She has been in the Prairieland Detention Center in Alvarado ever since.

“I’m scared to get deported,” Li said in an interview from Prairieland.

That’s because she and her family are Christians — which the Chinese government surveils and prosecutes.

“As a child, she experienced severe religious persecution, including physical assaults after teachers targeted her because she was the daughter of a Christian minister,” said her husband, Nathaniel Clemetson. “In one incident, she was dragged by her hair down a flight of stairs.”

She immigrated from China to the U.S. in 2019 on a student visa and moved to Texas to study early childhood education at Dallas Baptist University. She then transferred to the Academy of Art in San Francisco because she wanted to pursue a bachelor of fine arts in acting.

With in-person classes cancelled during the COVID-19 pandemic, she returned to Texas to do online courses.

But in 2022, she started showing symptoms of depression — trouble sleeping, avoiding socializing and not eating. Her doctor wrote her a medical note to excuse her from school, explaining that her bipolar disorder was causing her to have stress and depression. Her doctor wrote that she needed to take care of her mental health before she returned to school.

But her mental health struggles worsened, she said.

That summer she said she twice attempted suicide — the first time, she intended to jump off a multi-story parking garage, but said a Chinese worship song suddenly came to her mind, reminding her that only God can take her life. The second time, she said she took more than 50,000 milligrams of her prescribed sleeping medication. Three days later, she woke up in a hospital intensive care unit, where she recovered.

By this time, her mother, a Christian minister, left China seeking political asylum in the U.S. Her mother moved in with Li in Dallas and eventually won her asylum case; she’s now waiting on her legal permanent residency card.

Her mother’s constant presence “and God’s love, got me out of my depression,” she said.

She said she realized she had overstayed her visa but didn’t want to go back to China out of fear of being persecuted.

Then in late 2025, Li went to a line dancing class at a bar in Fort Worth. There she met Clemetson, who describes himself as a traditional Christian like Li. In February, they got married.

Clemetson, who was born and raised in Denton, said he and Li began the process of applying for her legal permanent residence — as a U.S. citizen he could sponsor her. He said they were gathering evidence that their marriage was real and saving money to pay for the required medical examination fee and file the application with immigration services.

But ICE arrested her before they could file, he said, and the officers didn’t care that they were married and trying to get Li a green card.

“They said that that didn’t matter, that we could sort that out in immigration court,” he said.

Since Li’s arrest, Clemetson has kickstarted an online campaign — creating a website and sharing anecdotes on videos uploaded to his social media profiles — to bring awareness to his wife’s detention and what she could face if she’s deported to China.

Li has been in immigration custody for 125 days and has a deportation order because she overstayed her student visa after leaving school. Her immigration lawyer has appealed the deportation order.

She said she misses her workout routines with her husband and going to her Arlington church, where she was part of the worship team and attended Bible study and the marriage group.

And she misses cooking with her mom.

“With my mom, we would cook traditional Chinese food,” she said. “There’s just different ways to, like, make some soup and noodles, rice, and I mean we just make dumplings from scratch together.”

“When I was outside, I would take many things for granted,” she said.

Her experience in detention has changed her perspective on life, she said.

“When I got here, I was like, ‘Wow, so many little stuff I was able to do outside, so easy to do outside,’” she said. “I lost all those privileges. I know when I get out from this detention center, I will be really much grateful.”

Octavio Daniel Cabrera Valdez, 36, Mexico

He escaped cartels in Mexico and applied for a green card, only to be arrested in San Antonio

By Alejandro SantosCid

Seconds after Octavio Daniel Cabrera Valdez noticed the truck tailing him through the streets of Monclova, Mexico, its passengers pointed rifles at him and signaled him to stop.

He sped up. The truck followed.

Cabrera Valdez managed to lose them, then pulled up to a house under construction, hid his car and climbed to the second floor. From the window, Cabrera Valdez watched the truck pass by, searching for him.

“I saw them stop in the middle of the street. There were a few young guys there on the sidewalks. They grabbed them by the hands and feet, loaded them onto their trucks,” Cabrera Valdez recalls. “I heard their mothers screaming.”

Those who were taken away didn’t return.

It wasn’t the first time, but Cabrera Valdez decided it would be the last. In those years — the late 2010s — the Zetas, army deserters who recycled themselves into a drug cartel, ruled over Coahuila. Cabrera Valdez’ family ran a scrapyard in Monclova, his hometown. The Zetas would extort them into destroying stolen cars that they had used for God only knows what. Cabrera Valdez could take it, but his little boy had just been born.

“I made the decision to pack my whole life into some suitcases, and let’s go. My son depends on me. It’s a life I have in my hands,” he says.

In 2020, Cabrera Valdez, his wife and his son entered the U.S. through Eagle Pass as tourists. He had been crossing back and forth since he was a baby; his parents, siblings and grandparents had lived in San Antonio for years and most of them were American citizens.

So they headed to San Antonio. After their visas expired, they stayed. Their second child was born there. Cabrera Valdez worked long hours installing fiber-optic cable, played bass in a local church, felt at ease. He applied for a green card through his mother, who is a citizen, and was waiting for the government to take action.

On April 17, Cabrera Valdez said, a police officer approached him and some co-workers on at a job site and asked for their papers. He was put in handcuffs, then turned over to Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which sent him to the Karnes City detention facility southeast of San Antonio. He’s been there ever since.

Homeland Security said the Stockdale Marshall’s Office arrested Cabrera Valdez and turned him over to ICE as part of an immigration enforcement collaboration.

“They’re hunting, just like the cartels down in Mexico. Here they’re hunting workers,” Cabrera Valdez says.

He shares a cell with seven detainees. Food is scarce, so he’s always hungry. In the evenings, the cellmates collect the little money they have from working in the kitchen — one dollar an hour, three hours a day — to buy noodles, sausages, refried beans.

That’s not the worst part, he says.

He’s had a constant rash that he thinks is from sharing his bed with insects. He can only wash his clothes with hot water, no soap, and he believes that makes it worse.

Sometimes he gets bad migraines. Once he asked for a pill. The guard instructed him to fill out a form. Twelve hours later, they gave him medicine.

“They try to humiliate you psychologically, as if you were a criminal,” Cabrera Valdez says.

Sometimes he feels like screaming.

His older son, who’s 8, had a plan to sell all his toys, the house furniture, everything, to get his dad out of jail. If that doesn’t work, he may even become a youtuber.

Without Cabrera Valdez’ salary to pay the bills, his wife ended up selling everything and moving to another part of Texas with their sons, where other family members support them. They speak daily by phone, but stopped visiting. Cabrera Valdez says they are in hiding, afraid of going out where ICE or police could arrest them.

By now his son has realized his plan didn’t play out as expected. He doesn’t understand why his father is still behind bars even after he sold his toys.

That is, Cabrera Valdez says, the worst part.

“They’re not taking the worst of the United States like they said,” he says. “They’re taking away a lot of people who are trying to contribute to this nation that belongs to our children.”

Shahrokh Rahimi, 54, Iran

Tortured in Iran for opposing the government, he’s spent 15 months in ICE detention in Texas

By Alex Nguyen

For more than a year, one question has nagged at Shahrokh Rahimi: Why is he in ICE detention?

The 54-year-old said he fled Iran over two decades ago after being detained and tortured for opposing the government. In 2003, he crossed into the U.S. illegally before settling in San Antonio, where he worked at a gas station and later a Mexican restaurant.

Then Rahimi met his now-wife, a U.S. citizen and daycare director who encouraged him to fix his immigration status. He applied for asylum in 2009, the same year they got married, but the U.S. government denied his application in 2010 because he didn’t submit it within one year of entering the country.

But he also couldn’t be deported back to Iran, where he could be persecuted again, an immigration judge ruled.

Instead Rahimi spent the next 15 years building a new life under an order of supervision, which allows immigrants with a final removal order to live in the country while being monitored by ICE.

He worked as a cook at his wife’s daycare center, a manager of a small breakfast and lunch place, and later a caregiver for military veterans in their homes. He got involved in his church after converting to Christianity. He also became the ultimate family man, never going out without his wife and daughter, always being the one to pick his 12-year-old up from school.

He also dutifully went to weekly ICE check-ins that tapered over time to yearly visits, and avoided any trouble with the law beyond a speeding ticket that was dismissed.

But all that didn’t matter on the morning of June 22, 2025, when ICE officers came knocking on his door and led him away in handcuffs.

“My wife and my daughter were just freaking out,” he recalled in a recent phone interview. “I was so scared.”

For the first few months, Rahimi was mostly held at a detention center in Pearsall, south of San Antonio, crying when he talked on the phone with his family. Meanwhile, the Texas Civil Rights Project was fighting in federal court to get him out, arguing that the government’s mandatory detention policy violates the law and his right to due process.

In early December, a federal judge ordered that Rahimi be given a bond hearing, raising hope that he could get home in time for Christmas. That wish was dashed just days later when an immigration judge said he was a flight risk, his wife, Brandi Rahimi wrote in her Gofundme campaign.

Then, just before the new year, ICE moved him to a facility in Karnes City.

Dog food is better than what he receives at the new facility, Rahimi said. Guards routinely curse at him, he added.

So he spends his days chatting with his daughter and studying the Bible, he says, trying to not let the conditions break his spirit. Still, his long stay in detention baffles him and his wife.

“I didn’t do anything wrong to deserve to be [held] one year in detention,” Rahimi said.

On the outside, money has gotten tight for his family. His car was repossessed. And after the Iran war sent gas prices soaring, Rahimi told his wife to make the hour-long drive to visit him less often.

“It’s the one time once a week that we get to see you for an hour,” she would respond. “No, it’s worth it for me to come.”

In July, the TCRP filed a new lawsuit to again challenge Rahimi’s detention. It was still pending as of Sept. 21.

“I just want to go back to my family,” Rahimi said.

Yeferson Francisco Sequera Ruiz, 31, Venezuela

Stripped of legal status on Trump’s first day in office, he was taken away in chains “like a dog”

By Alejandro SantosCid

Yeferson Francisco Sequera Ruiz sat in the back of a car with two U.S. citizens on their way to a job at a ranch when a state trooper stopped them outside Austin on Nov. 6.

The 31-year-old Venezuelan, whom everyone calls Yefri, had an appointment three days later for his work permit. He was afraid of working before getting his papers in order, but the rancher — who knew Yefri, his wife and three daughters were struggling — would give him small jobs and pay with food, clothes, a little money.

The trooper checked their papers.

Ten minutes later two black vans arrived. ICE handcuffed Sequera Ruiz and chained his waist, feet, and hands. “Like a dog,” he said.

“I cried,” he said, “because I’m 31 and I’d never been detained.”

They took him to the T. Don Hutto Detention Center in Taylor.

“All I did was cry and ask myself, ‘Yeferson, what bad things did you do to end up here?’” he said. “It wasn’t a detention center — it was a prison.”

He and his family had left Venezuela in 2019. The work on his parents’ farm didn’t pay much, and they feared reprisals after joining protests against the government over lack of food and health care in the struggling nation. After fleeing to Colombia for a few years, they headed north in 2024.

His daughters nearly died crossing the Darién Gap, the roadless jungle between Colombia and Panama, where thirst made them drink from a river littered with the bodies of decomposing immigrants.

Finally, on Oct. 25, 2024, they walked legally into Eagle Pass after waiting nine months in Mexico for an asylum appointment with a U.S. official.

Three months later President Donald Trump stripped Sequera Ruiz’s family and about another million immigrants of legal status on his first day in office.

The family settled in San Antonio, working odd jobs when they could and sheltering in churches until a pastor helped them rent a small apartment.

In the detention center, Sequera Ruiz said he shared a cell with another man, slept on a mattress that was as hard as the floor and covered himself with blankets so thin he could see through them.

“The food and the water were so bad they made you sick. The air conditioners blew out dust. If you wake up with a cold, you’d hold back from going to the doctor because they would confine you for five days.”

A judge tried to deport Sequera Ruiz to Ecuador, a country he didn’t know, but his lawyer appealed.

As the months passed, Sequera Ruiz said he witnessed other detainees losing their minds, attempting to take their own lives, believing all was lost — “because, in there, everything is lost.”

He kept himself sane by talking to his family every day through the tablets the detainees could rent. His daughters — now 8, 10 and 14 — visited twice, but the officers didn’t let Sequera Ruiz hug them or hold their hands.

“They graduated from school and their father wasn’t there, just because ICE gets a kick out of detaining innocent people.”

For Father’s Day, one of his daughters drew a picture of the family that depicted her father as a face on a tablet screen. Sequera Ruiz said he survived by reading the Bible, asking God for strength and a chance.

It arrived eight months after his arrest when a judge granted his habeas corpus petition challenging detention.

He spent the last night in his cell looking at the window, feeling like the minutes wouldn’t end.

On July 7, he walked out of the detention center with a one-year parole. He hugged his daughters again.

text:
A trio of news outlets President Trump barred from covering the White House last week sued the administration on Monday, arguing it is violating the First Amendment and harming their ability to share information about the government with the public.

In the lawsuit, filed in district court in Washington, D.C., attorneys for CNN, MS NOW and Politico argued the ban “could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles.”

The block “retaliates against protected newsgathering and speech in violation of the First Amendment,” the suit argues, noting Trump’s statements about the outlets he banned make “clear he implemented the ban to coerce more favorable coverage of the administration from CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, and to deter other journalists and news organizations from reporting that the President might view as unfavorable.”

The president on Friday said the outlets were banned from the White House after publishing what he called “fake news” — a move that has been widely condemned by First Amendment advocates and other media organizations.

On Monday, the TV pool that covers the president’s daily movements said it was boycotting those responsibilities in a show of solidarity with CNN, one of its member outlets.

“The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government,” the networks wrote in a joint statement. “No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”

The president’s ban is “already severely impeding the ability of CNN, MS NOW, and

POLITICO to cover the President and his administration,” the lawsuit argues asking the court to “immediately enjoin enforcement of the ban.”

The case has been assigned to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, the same judge who oversaw the White House’s temporary ban on a press credential belonging to former CNN reporter Jim Acosta during Trump’s first term.

Trump earlier Monday sought to justify the ban in a post on Truth Social.

“The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” he wrote, arguing the administration is instead “instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS.”

“It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control,” the president continued. “It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”

title: A Timeline of Badar Khan Suri's Legal Battle - The Hoya
description:
Badar Khan Suri came to the United States in 2022 to research democracy and minority rights at Georgetown University.
Though a federal judge released Khan Suri almost two months after he was detained, the Georgetown researcher remains embroiled in a two-pronged legal fight.
In immigration court, meanwhile, Khan Suri continues to dispute the government’s removal case, arguing against a November 2025 ruling that he is deportable.
Khan Suri said the last year and a half have been exhausting.
“It’s a long struggle,” Khan Suri told The Hoya in April 2026.
text:
Badar Khan Suri came to the United States in 2022 to research democracy and minority rights at Georgetown University. He had been writing a book on Indian nationalism for over two years when federal immigration authorities detained him in March 2025, alleging he threatened U.S. foreign policy goals.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security cited online posts about him and his connection to his father-in-law — a former Hamas official — to argue that Khan Suri was spreading “Hamas propaganda” and antisemitism. He denies these allegations, and the government has published limited evidence to support its claims.

Though a federal judge released Khan Suri almost two months after he was detained, the Georgetown researcher remains embroiled in a two-pronged legal fight.

In September, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to review a July appeals court’s ruling that Khan Suri can remain free from detention while his immigration case proceeds. Because the appellate ruling split from two other appeals courts’ rulings in similar cases, the Supreme Court is more likely to hear the challenge.

In immigration court, meanwhile, Khan Suri continues to dispute the government’s removal case, arguing against a November 2025 ruling that he is deportable.

Though The Hoya attended Khan Suri’s first-ever immigration trial this September, the proceedings remain relatively opaque — judges do not publish their dockets or decisions. The immigration judge has yet to decide the case, but Khan Suri’s lawyers expect an unfavorable verdict.

Khan Suri said the last year and a half have been exhausting.

“It’s a long struggle,” Khan Suri told The Hoya in April 2026. “When I returned home, I knew that I’m still in the desert, so I don’t know if I’m seeing an oasis or a mirage. It could be anything. If I’m in a sea, I’m drowning. My head is out, but still I’m in a big sea.”

name: Litigation
title: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to hear challenge to Badar Khan Suri's case
authors: Sydney Carroll, Sarah Watson, Editorial Board, Angelena Bougiamas
description: U.S. government lawyers asked the U.S. Supreme Court on Monday to hear their appeal in Trump v. Khan Suri.
text:
Lawyers for the U.S. government asked the U.S. Supreme Court on Monday to hear their appeal in Trump v. Khan Suri, arguing that previous courts lacked the jurisdiction to hear his legal challenges to his detention. They argue that the Supreme Court must decide whether noncitizens’ claims of unlawful detention can be heard in federal court after multiple circuit courts came to different conclusions.

Lawyers for the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) argue that the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) mandates that courts do not have jurisdiction to review “any other cause or claim arising from or relating to the implementation or operation of an order of removal.”

“Those claims—which go to the validity of his apprehension, detention, and removal in equal force—all stem from respondent’s objection to being placed in removal proceedings in the first place. That is, his challenge to his detention is entirely derivative of his challenge to his being removed,” the DOJ wrote in their petition to the Supreme Court.

Khan Suri was detained outside his home in March 2025 while residing in the U.S. legally on a J-1 exchange visa, issued to teachers, students, and scholars. After spending 58 days in ICE detention, federal Judge Patricia Tolliver Giles ruled that Khan Suri needed to be released on bond. In July, a federal appeals court ruled that he should remain out of detention while his case proceeds.

The DOJ argues that Khan Suri could still contest his detention through the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) while also contesting his deportation. However, Khan Suri’s lawyers have argued that a challenge to his detention is necessary and separate from his removal proceedings, because by the time his removal case is decided, he will have already suffered a separate and undue harm through an extended detention. Judge DeAndrea Benjamin of the Fourth Circuit agreed with this assessment in her opinion in July.

“If a noncitizen is challenging their detention pending removal, then waiting for their removal proceedings does them no good,” Benjamin wrote. “They have already been detained, allegedly in violation of the Constitution. This ‘absurd’ reading of the INA would make such detention claims ‘effectively unreviewable.’”

Khan Suri is currently undergoing two different court cases. The first case, which has been appealed to the Supreme Court, addressed if Khan Suri’s detention itself was legal, which his lawyers argue acted as a retaliation against his support for Palestine and marriage to a Palestinian. He is also undergoing a separate immigration case, which determines whether the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) can deport him.

The Fourth Circuit’s 2-1 decision in favor of Khan Suri created a circuit split, or disagreement between federal courts in different cases on the same issue. Khan Suri is one of many individuals across the country fighting their detention in court. In January 2026, the Third Circuit ruled in the case of Columbia University graduate Mahmoud Khalil that the INA does prohibit cases related to immigration detention from being heard in federal court, and in July, the Second Circuit ruled the same in the case of another Columbia student, Mohsen Mahdawi.

“This case presents an important question of immigration law that has divided the circuits: Must aliens challenge the grounds for their removal solely through the petition-for-review process that Congress prescribed under Title 8 of the U.S. Code, or can aliens detained pending removal proceedings file habeas petitions that collaterally attack the bases for those removal proceedings?” the Department of Justice wrote.

Instead, the DOJ argues that a section of the INA that strips district courts of jurisdiction over “nearly all” claims “arising from removal proceedings,” therefore bars Khan Suri from “collaterally challenging the bases for [his] removal by filing habeas petitions that raise the same basic claims just as defects to their detention.”

In cases where there is a circuit split, the Supreme Court is typically asked to intervene to issue the ultimate national ruling on the matter. However, the Trump administration asking the Supreme Court to hear the case does not guarantee that they will do so—the court receives over 10,000 petitions every year and typically only hears around 65-70 cases. Once the petition is received, four of the court’s nine justices must determine that the case has merit for them to review in order for it to enter the Supreme Court’s docket.

Khan Suri believes that his case has a good chance at being selected because of its wide-reaching implications.

“They will do it, because they want a precedent that no immigration related case should be decided through habeas in federal court,” Khan Suri said on Monday night at a teach-in about his case.

The DOJ concurred in their petition.

“The question presented is remarkably important. Whether an alien can collaterally attack his removal by filing a habeas petition challenging his detention potentially affects thousands upon thousands of cases, well beyond the immediate fact pattern at issue here,” they wrote.

They also argued that upholding the Fourth Circuit’s decision could allow other noncitizens to cite Khan Suri’s case as precedent. They continue that, “left unchecked, such suits risk producing an overwhelming litigation burden on both the government and the courts.”

Lawyers for Khalil have also appealed his case to the Supreme Court, which means the court will likely decide between the two cases, or hear neither. Khalil’s case is broader than Khan Suri’s, covering both his detention and elements of the government’s attempts to deport him. However, the DOJ also argued that the court should take both cases, arguing that “doing so would guard against the possibility of mootness present in cases like this, where removal proceedings remain ongoing.”

The Supreme Court has been a mixed bag in ruling on cases related to immigration as of late. The court upheld birthright citizenship in Trump v. Barbara in June, but also allowed the Trump administration to end removal protections for Syrian and Haitian nationals in Mullen v. Doe and also allowed the administration to revive restrictions on the amount of people who can apply for asylum each day in Mullin v. Al Otro Lado.

Khan Suri said on Monday night that he remains hopeful that his case will continue to succeed.

“I am 100% sure that someday, sometime, justice will prevail,” he said.

name: Human Rights
title: The National Security Exception Was Never Going to Stop at Prosecuting Muslims | Truthout
authors: Zack Kligler, Sufia Khalid, Nabil Salih, Maya Schenwar, Khury Petersen-Smith, Maha Hilal, Negin Owliaei, Sharon Zhang, Mike Ludwig, Erin Rode
description:
Section 2339A criminalizes “material support” of terrorist acts, which includes property damage, for anyone — no organizational affiliation, foreign or domestic, is necessary.
The vagueness of this language grants broad discretion, and in national security cases, that discretion has never been exercised neutrally.
When a court accepts that a Muslim individual’s charity, business, or speech is terrorism, that ruling becomes law for everyone.

An injustice against Muslims was never going to remain an injustice against Muslims alone.
text:
Part of the Series

The War That Was Never Meant to End: 25 Years of the War on Terror

For 25 years, the US ran a parallel legal system largely for Muslims. It now reaches immigrants and the left.

Less than two weeks after the September 11, 2001, attacks, President George W. Bush told Congress that the war on terror “begins with al Qaeda, but it does not end there.” Twenty-five years later, his line reads as a confession: the war on terror was designed to have no borders and no end, and the legal machinery built to wage it at home was drafted in the same way.

In my work as a federal criminal defense and constitutional law attorney, I defend people unjustly prosecuted by that machinery. Until recently, most of my clients were Muslim. What their cases demonstrate is that after 9/11, the United States built a separate system of justice — a national security exception to the Constitution — that was largely tested on a population that was demonized by both the state and the media. While non-Muslims were assured it would never apply to them — and were repeatedly told not to worry about the creeping encroachment of the state if they had nothing to hide — that assurance has expired.

A Second-Class System of Justice

The national security exception to the Constitution operates through a variety of mechanisms: statutes vague enough to criminalize charity and speech; informants and undercover agents who manufacture crimes they later “disrupt”; classified evidence defendants cannot see; mass surveillance; and a sentencing enhancement that categorizes even first-time, nonviolent defendants as hardened career offenders. Each element was justified as an emergency measure, but none of them has expired.

In 2004, Justice Sandra Day O’Connor wrote in Hamdi v. Rumsfeld (a Supreme Court case that found that American citizens detained from an active combat zone as enemy combatants retain the right to due process and a meaningful opportunity to challenge the factual basis of their detention before a neutral decision-maker) that “a state of war is not a blank check for the President when it comes to the rights of the Nation’s citizens.” But for Muslims in U.S. courtrooms, it has functioned as one. Sixty years earlier, dissenting in Korematsu v. United States, in which the Supreme Court upheld the internment of over 120,000 Japanese Americans during World War II, Justice Robert Jackson warned that a principle of discrimination, once blessed by the courts, “lies about like a loaded weapon, ready for the hand of any authority that can bring forward a plausible claim of an urgent need,” and that “every repetition imbeds that principle more deeply in our law and thinking and expands it to new purposes.”

We have been living inside that warning, with the guise of “national security” as the ever-prevailing “urgent need.”

Laws Written to Be Expanded

The statutes criminalizing the “material support” of terrorism sit at the center of the exception. Under the U.S. federal criminal code, Section 2339B of Title 18 makes it a felony to provide “material support or resources” to any group the secretary of state designates a foreign terrorist organization, with no requirement that the defendant intended to further violence or that anything they provided was ever used for such purpose. Section 2339A criminalizes “material support” of terrorist acts, which includes property damage, for anyone — no organizational affiliation, foreign or domestic, is necessary. After 9/11, Congress added “expert advice or assistance,” to the definition of material support, extended the law to “any property, tangible or intangible, or service,” and increased the maximum sentence for Section 2339B to 20 years. In Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project, the Supreme Court held in 2010 that even teaching members of designated groups to peacefully use international law and petition the United Nations could be prosecuted as support for terrorism.

The vagueness of this language grants broad discretion, and in national security cases, that discretion has never been exercised neutrally. When a statute can be interpreted to apply to a donation, a translation, a social media post, or group chat, it introduces ambiguity. The decisive question becomes not what a person did but whom the government decides that person to be, or what that person is associated with, leaving prosecutors free to target particular religious communities, political viewpoints, and speech while insisting they are simply enforcing the law.

Whatever policy aims these prosecutions served, their political function was hard to dispute. Every “foiled plot” announced at a press conference reinforced a story in which the enemy was Muslim, already among us, and defeatable only through wars abroad and extraordinary powers at home.

That story helped sell wars built on falsehoods, including the invasion of Iraq, premised on weapons of mass destruction that did not exist. Brown University’s Costs of War Project estimates that more than 940,000 people were killed by direct violence in the post-9/11 war zones through 2023, with more than 432,000 of them civilians, and total deaths reaching 4.5 to 4.7 million.

Domestically, the “Muslim terrorist” narrative regularly painted by state officials and the media also gave permission to non-Muslim people to look the other way, casting suspicion on an entire religion instead of scrutinizing how these legal exceptions were operating. As a result, for two decades, the government largely took aim at Muslims, with little notice from broader society — until these powers and statutes were applied to less marginalized groups and people whose political leanings have fallen out of favor.

How the Machinery Was Built

From 2001 to 2025, the FBI’s counterterrorism budget tripled, and informants were sent in droves into mosques. A 2014 Human Rights Watch and Columbia Law School report found that nearly half of more than 500 federal counterterrorism convictions came from informant-based cases. Almost 30 percent of them were stings in which the informant actively shaped the plot for which the person was prosecuted.

The Holy Land Foundation, once the largest Muslim charity in the country, became the template: its leaders were prosecuted over donations to local charity committees in Gaza that appeared on no U.S. terrorist list, and after a first trial ended without a single conviction, the five men were sentenced in 2009 on retrial to up to 65 years. Paying religiously mandated charity to support orphans could now make Muslims suspects.

As the government continued focusing its purported “counterterrorism” efforts on Muslims, including in United States v. Adel Daoud and United States v. Tarek Mehanna, its own analysts documented a deadlier threat it pursued with far less zeal. A 2017 Government Accountability Office report attributed 73 percent of deadly violent extremist incidents between 9/11 and the end of 2016 to far right extremists, and in 2020 the Department of Homeland Security called white supremacist extremists “the most persistent and lethal threat in the Homeland.” Even after the 2017 report, the vast majority of counterterrorism investigations and prosecutions were brought against Muslims instead.

What It Looks Like From the Defense Table

In my work at the National Security Criminal Defense Center at the Muslim Legal Fund of America, we have defended against the expansion and abuse of this post-9/11 legal machinery. In 2019, Imad Eddin Wadi, a Syrian-born American with no criminal record and no history of violence, needed investors for a halal slaughterhouse business venture. An FBI informant introduced him to the representative of a wealthy “Kuwaiti sheikh,” whom the Fifth Circuit itself described as “FBI-concocted.” The invented sheikh offered Wadi $9 million on the condition that a share go to a Syrian armed group (the group was undesignated but the government argued the individuals were part of a designated terrorist organization, known then as Jabhat al-Nusra and more recently as Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham). Due to this plot directed by the FBI, Wadi was sentenced to 160 months in federal prison. Before trial, the informant, an undercover FBI agent, replaced the phone he used throughout the operation, violating a court evidence preservation order, and the courts refused to give any sanction or remedy. We asked the Supreme Court whether the government escapes accountability when its informant wipes important evidence in defiance of a court order; in June of this year, it declined to hear the case.

In July 2025, the State Department revoked the terrorist designation of Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham. The group’s leader until its disbanding, Mohammed Al-Jolani (now rebranded as Ahmad al-Sharaa) is now the president of Syria and was invited in 2025 to the White House. Meanwhile, Wadi remains in prison.

Jason Fong, a Chinese American Marine Corps reservist, drew federal attention for joining online discussions of a possible American civil war only after he converted to Islam in 2020. Undercover operatives spent months trying to draw him into a crime. After sharing PDF materials and a fundraising link for Hamas upon their request, he was charged with material support offenses carrying up to 80 years. During Fong’s trial, the covert FBI employee’s problematic tactics were exposed, including the in-person contact between the adult FBI employee and a minor child that involved driving around together and radicalizing discussion, without parental knowledge. Prosecutors there offered to dismiss every material support count in exchange for a false statement plea.

These kinds of informant stings often target the most vulnerable. As reported by The Intercept, FBI agents posing as Islamic State contacts began communicating with Humzah Mashkoor, a teenager diagnosed with autism, when he was 16. He was arrested for attempted material support to a terrorist organization weeks after turning 18. In another case, Davin Meyer’s mother reported her son, who was autistic and suffering from mental health issues, to local authorities hoping to get him help; paid FBI informants began cultivating him soon after his 18th birthday and helped him plan a trip abroad to join a terrorist organization that ended in his arrest. As his lawyer put it in court, the government “fanned the flames of what they condemn now.”

Hanging over all of these cases is the federal terrorism sentencing enhancement, the most severe sentencing enhancement that was promulgated without any evidentiary basis. This sentencing enhancement is discriminatorily applied and requires only that the offense was calculated to influence or affect the conduct of government through intimidation, retaliation, or coercion. It results in a recommended maximum sentence in every case and a recommended 360 months to life sentence in any material support case, including for purely online, nonviolent, first-time offense conduct. As I have documented for the U.S. Sentencing Commission, the terrorism sentencing enhancement adds 12 offense levels on top of the base offense level and assigns the criminal history category reserved for “career offenders,” producing a minimum guideline range of 17.5 years and usually a recommended range of 360 months to life. This puts immense pressure on defendants to plead guilty and forego their constitutional rights to a fair trial and to confront the evidence against them.

A system that was built for persecuting one disfavored group is always going to seek out others. This legal machinery has been turned on Venezuelan migrants who have been labeled gang members under the Alien Enemies Act, on Palestine solidarity activists, and on the left. In September 2025, President Donald Trump declared “antifa” a domestic terrorist organization, though no statute authorizes such a designation, and National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 directed the offices of the FBI Counterterrorism’s Joint Terrorism Task Forces and newly created Joint Task Force Vanguard, to pursue organizations and funders animated by “anti-Americanism, anti-capitalism, and anti-Christianity” and “extremism on migration, race, and gender.” Muslims were not replaced as targets but folded in: the administration designated several more Muslim organizations and a vast majority of Palestinian civil society organizations.

In June of this year, federal judges in Fort Worth sentenced seven defendants in the Prairieland Detention Center case, the Justice Department’s first antifa prosecution of 16 noise demonstrators, to 30 to 100 years, though only one person was convicted of the shooting that injured one officer outside the immigrant jail (the officer receive sutures and made a full recovery). Indeed, one of the people charged did not even attend the demonstration but simply moved a box of zines and personal documents in its wake, and the others who received 50-70 years were not involved when shot was fired. I represent one of those defendants, Maricela Rueda, on appeal. Every tool used in that case was developed, tested, and normalized in the prosecutions of Muslims.

Precedents Come For Us All

Both ignorance and fear, fed by popular entertainment depicting Muslims as terrorists and right-wing commentators pushing racist propaganda like the “great replacement” conspiracy theory, have kept most Americans from diving into the legal mechanisms behind these cases. Administrations change; precedents do not. The system used against Muslims yesterday and leftists today will belong to whoever holds power next.

The Constitution protects no one on its own; it did not stop Japanese American internment or the people targeted by FBI’s COINTELPRO, and its guarantees have been real only when people and movements have forced the government to honor them. When a court accepts that a Muslim individual’s charity, business, or speech is terrorism, that ruling becomes law for everyone. The ground Muslim defendants lost is the ground all of us were standing on.

Frederick Douglass warned in 1857 that if you “find out just what any people will quietly submit to,” you will have found “the exact measure of injustice and wrong which will be imposed upon them.” For 25 years, the measure of what Americans would quietly submit to was taken in regard to Muslims.

Changing this system must begin where the exception began: with the word “terrorism” itself. Our legal system does not objectively define the term, and its use turns mostly on one’s ideology or identity rather than on any intent to further exceptional violence. The terrorism enhancement puts immense pressure on defendants to plead guilty and avoid a maximum sentence exposure after trial due to its draconian sentencing provisions. Its discriminatory application should be measured and exposed and eliminated. We need to roll back the vast powers exercised by inter-agency Joint Terrorism Task Forces and the veil of classification that lays over “national security” cases. Until then, everyone charged under this regime deserves a trial that forces the government to actually prove its case, rather than pushing a narrative based on decades of racialized hate.

An injustice against Muslims was never going to remain an injustice against Muslims alone. Whatever one’s politics, these precedents will eventually be wielded by an unfriendly administration against one’s community. Reforming the legal machinery of the war on terror is the only protection any of us will have when the next authority arrives with “a plausible claim of an urgent need.”

name: Human Rights
title: Ohio taxpayers face a $1670 deportation bill, and a smaller workforce
authors: Richard T. Herman, Megan Henry, Marty Schladen
description:
The methodology allocates a projected $268.9 billion federal cost according to each state’s share of federal income taxes.
That is an allocation of projected federal spending, not a new charge on an Ohio tax return.
But Ohioans will pay again if enforcement removes workers and destabilizes the families, businesses and tax base Ohio needs to grow.
Ohio’s workforce already depends on immigrants.
He and JobsOhio should say plainly that broad removal undermines Ohio’s workforce strategy.
text:
An Economic Policy Institute calculator, as reported by Axios, estimates that the average Ohio federal income-tax filer who owes tax after credits would shoulder about $1,670 to finance President Donald Trump’s mass-deportation campaign.

The methodology allocates a projected $268.9 billion federal cost according to each state’s share of federal income taxes. Ohio’s share is nearly $6.9 billion through the remainder of Trump’s term.

That is an allocation of projected federal spending, not a new charge on an Ohio tax return. But Ohioans will pay again if enforcement removes workers and destabilizes the families, businesses and tax base Ohio needs to grow.

The administration says its enforcement targets the “worst of the worst.” The available Ohio data show a broader reach.

A review of federal records found that ICE detained 7,756 people in Ohio between January 2025 and March 2026. Fewer than 5% had been convicted of a violent offense; 47% had no criminal history. Some had pending charges or nonviolent convictions, including traffic-related offenses such as driving without a license.

People who present genuine threats should remain enforcement priorities, but these figures do not describe a narrowly targeted public-safety operation.

Detention is not deportation, but it often becomes the route to removal.

A Deportation Data Project analysis found that, among people with no criminal conviction or preexisting final removal order, the share deported within the first 60 days after being booked into detention roughly doubled during the administration’s first year.

People may also be detained for immigration-status violations — such as a visa overstay or the expiration of temporary protection — that are not criminal convictions.

Families separated, children losing parents, and neighbors disappearing are the human costs. The economic costs are also measurable.

A May 2026 OhioMeansJobs snapshot listed 126,739 online job postings, including 4,596 for registered nurses. The report cautions that postings are not a complete count of unique vacancies, but they show employer demand.

Ohio’s workforce already depends on immigrants. They make up 15.7% of personal-care aides, 9.1% of transportation and warehousing workers, 7.6% of manufacturing workers, 6.9% of agricultural workers and 6.2% of construction workers, compared with 6.2% of Ohio’s workforce overall, according to an American Immigration Council analysis.

The American Immigration Council’s definition includes naturalized citizens, lawful permanent residents, temporary visa holders, refugees, asylees and undocumented immigrants. Not every worker is subject to deportation.

The point is how deeply immigration is woven into Ohio’s workforce. Removing or stripping work authorization from even a fraction of these workers can mean longer waits for home care, delayed construction and production, higher business costs and higher prices for consumers.

Established companies are unlikely to move a factory overnight. The more realistic risk is lost work and lost investment.

A 2026 National Bureau of Economic Research working paper found that for every six likely undocumented men who lost employment after increased ICE activity, one U.S.-born man without a college degree also lost employment.

When employers cannot find workers, they may cut production, turn down work or place the next expansion where labor is easier to find.

Immigrant households also support Ohio’s public finances. In 2023, they paid $7.3 billion in federal, state, and local taxes and retained $20 billion in spending power, according to the American Immigration Council.

Entrepreneurs are a separate economic asset. More than 38,200 immigrant entrepreneurs — 8.2% of Ohio’s entrepreneurs — generated $1 billion in business income in 2023.

They create jobs, fill storefronts and strengthen local tax bases. A state that makes immigrant families feel unwelcome risks losing not only current workers, but also the next generation of business owners.

Ohio’s population story is uneven. JobsOhio’s summary of new Census estimates says the state added 101,065 residents since 2020, with net migration contributing 146,471.

Census estimates put Cleveland’s 2025 population at 363,608, 2.4% below its 2020 base. Older cities and rural communities need residents to occupy homes, support schools and sustain local businesses.

I helped found Global Cleveland because a region that had lost population could not afford to treat newcomers as a threat. That was economic self-preservation.

JobsOhio understands the competition. It offers up to $15,000 for each qualifying out-of-state STEM or technical hire above an employer’s three-year baseline.

Paying companies to recruit workers while spending billions to drive other workers away is not a coherent development strategy.

Immigration is not a substitute for better wages, safer workplaces or serious training for Ohioans.

Ohio should invest in all three while enforcing against genuine threats. But Gov. Mike DeWine has acknowledged that Ohio needs immigrants. He and JobsOhio should say plainly that broad removal undermines Ohio’s workforce strategy.

The state’s congressional delegation should press for legal employment channels that match workforce needs, dependable seasonal-worker programs and a workable legal-status process for long-settled residents without serious criminal records.

Ohio cannot recruit workers, attract investment, and repopulate communities while paying nearly $6.9 billion to make itself smaller.
