text:
Whistleblower alleges admin weaponizes FOIA to sabotage immigrants’ cases

The largest category of Freedom of Information Act requesters is noncitizens seeking copies of their immigration records, known as A-files. These requesters accounted for the bulk of the more than one million FOIA requests received by the Department of Homeland Security last year. Because FOIA requests are often the only way to obtain documentation required to prove or maintain legal status, any delay or change to the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ FOIA office can imperil hundreds of thousands of applicants and asylum seekers.

A landmark 2020 ruling, Nightingale v. USCIS, which was the first class action FOIA case, found that the agency had a pattern of violating the act, and required it going forward to process FOIA requests for A-files in 30 days and maintain a zero-case backlog. (The court rightly noted that if an agency aggressively increases its immigration enforcement, it should similarly increase its capacity to process requests for information concerning immigration status.)

It appears USCIS is not following the court’s order. A recent whistleblower complaint and amicus brief filed by the Government Accountability Project argues that the agency is refusing to search for immigrants’ records unless the requests meet unreasonably strict criteria, and is misleading the court about its compliance with Nightingale.

The whistleblower complaint, filed by former USCIS records official Timothy Turner, alleged that the agency’s FOIA staff received several unlawful orders last year. Staff were instructed to:

Exclude searching for records that contain any common variation on the spelling of names (an absurd position to take, given that the government recognizes more than 70 different ways to spell Moammar Gadhafi).

Not release any documentation unless it was in English, even though immigration records often contain foreign languages.

Withhold evidence, like marriage certificates, tax forms, and hearing transcripts, by misapplying privacy exemptions.

Whether FOIA is the best process for requesting or releasing A-files is an open question, but until another system is built, the agency must comply with the current one.

USDA ignores FOIA request for a year, then threatens to close it in 4 days

The Department of Agriculture recently sent me a dreaded “still interested” letter regarding a nearly year-old FOIA request concerning Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program data. These are letters demanding that requesters reaffirm their interest in having their request processed, often after agencies have ignored them for months or years. Otherwise, their requests will be summarily closed. Nothing in the statute allows this practice, but “still interested” letters are a popular backlog-slashing tactic for agencies, especially as their resources have been slashed and we approach the end of the government’s fiscal year.

How long did USDA give me to respond? Four days. Even though I’d not heard anything from the agency in 10 months concerning my request, which sought information about the USDA’s chaotic November 2025 announcement prohibiting states from making full payments to the food assistance program.

The USDA’s response is almost as bad as the Army Corps of Engineers, which, just weeks ago, gave me only three days to confirm that I still wanted records related to reports the agency had raised the water level of a lake Vice President JD Vance used for a family kayaking trip.

Annoyed but undaunted, I immediately reminded USDA that agencies cannot lawfully close a request if they don’t receive a response to these letters, citing a recent ruling secured by American Oversight against the Energy Department underscoring this very point. I also pointed to Justice Department guidance stating agencies must use these letters sparingly and offer at least 30 days for requesters to respond.

Agencies either aren’t getting the message, they are willfully ignoring it, or they are being starved of resources they need to effectively engage with requesters.

Until the situation improves, requesters will have to keep doing the agencies’ job for them: reminding government officials what the law actually requires.

title: Two US deportees allegedly beaten in Equatorial Guinea after $7.5 million migration deal
description:
The allegations have placed renewed scrutiny on a controversial agreement under which the United States paid Equatorial Guinea $7.5 million to receive migrants deported under President Donald Trump’s third-country programme.
The money reportedly came from funds appropriated for migration and refugee assistance, although the people being sent to Equatorial Guinea were deportees rather than refugees receiving humanitarian support.
Washington has not disclosed complete public terms for the agreement, including how the money is being spent or what legal protections Equatorial Guinea promised to provide.
In May, United Nations human rights experts asked Equatorial Guinea not to return deportees to countries where they could be persecuted.
The US State Department it will continue using lawful measures to remove people who had no right to remain in the United States.
text:
Ahmed Soliman, a 31-year-old Egyptian, and Samson Birhane, a 47-year-old Eritrean, were arrested on September 11 and transferred to a prison in Malabo, according to lawyers and witnesses cited by the Associated Press⁠ and The Guardian⁠.

The allegations have placed renewed scrutiny on a controversial agreement under which the United States paid Equatorial Guinea $7.5 million to receive migrants deported under President Donald Trump’s third-country programme.

Neither the alleged assault nor the deportees’ treatment has been independently verified by Business Insider Africa.

ADVERTISEMENT

Men allegedly beaten over mobile phones

Witnesses said police accused the two men of damaging property at Hotel Bamy, a hotel outside Malabo that has been used to hold people deported from the United States.

The men were allegedly blindfolded or fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a staircase before being removed from the hotel.

Witnesses said officers repeatedly demanded the detainees' phone while assaulting the men.

Soliman had previously recorded police pointing guns at deportees during a dispute over confiscated mobile phones. The phones allowed the detainees to contact lawyers, relatives and journalists.

ADVERTISEMENT

Police later searched other rooms and confiscated additional devices, lawyers said.

“This is a human rights catastrophe,” said Bella Mosselmans, director of the Global Strategic Litigation Council, which represents several of the deportees.

Equatorial Guinea’s government had not publicly responded to the specific allegations at the time of the reports.

DON'T MISS THIS: Rwanda and 2 other African countries received over $20m from US in deportation deals, senate report says

Washington paid $7.5 million

ADVERTISEMENT

The United States transferred $7.5 million to Equatorial Guinea as part of its deportation cooperation agreement.

The money reportedly came from funds appropriated for migration and refugee assistance, although the people being sent to Equatorial Guinea were deportees rather than refugees receiving humanitarian support.

US Senator Jeanne Shaheen raised concerns about the payment in a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio. She said the transfer “raises serious concerns over the responsible, transparent use of American taxpayer dollars.”

The payment was particularly striking because it exceeded the total amount of US assistance reportedly provided to Equatorial Guinea during the previous eight years.

Washington has not disclosed complete public terms for the agreement, including how the money is being spent or what legal protections Equatorial Guinea promised to provide.

ADVERTISEMENT

At least 66 people from several countries, including African nations, Cuba and Brazil, have been sent to Equatorial Guinea since November 2025, according to Third Country Deportation Watch.

DON'T MISS THIS:Trump’s deportation program rewards African partners: $5.1m for Eswatini, $7.5m for Equatorial Guinea, Ghana gets visa relief

About 30 people remained at Hotel Bamy following the arrest of Soliman and Birhane.

Deportees left in legal limbo

Many of the deportees cannot safely return to their countries of origin because US immigration judges previously found that they could face persecution or torture there.

ADVERTISEMENT

Birhane arrived in the United States as a refugee at the age of 13. A judge later found that he faced a risk of torture in Eritrea.

Both men lost their US immigration status following criminal convictions, but had already served their sentences.

Lawyers say the deportees have been left in Equatorial Guinea without a clear immigration status, freedom of movement or a reliable process for securing legal protection elsewhere.

Some detainees have also reported limited access to medical treatment and clean clothing.

In May, United Nations human rights experts asked Equatorial Guinea not to return deportees to countries where they could be persecuted.

ADVERTISEMENT

DON'T MISS THIS:Five migrants who rejected Trump’s deportation to Liberia reportedly diverted to Equatorial Guinea

The African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights subsequently issued an interim order asking the government not to deport, transfer or relocate the individuals against their will.

US distances itself from conditions

US Immigration and Customs Enforcement has argued that its responsibility ends once deportees leave American custody.

“When an individual is no longer in ICE custody, ICE is no longer responsible for them,” an agency spokesperson told The Guardian.

ADVERTISEMENT

ICE maintained that all the deportees had been sent to what it considered a safe third country.

The US State Department it will continue using lawful measures to remove people who had no right to remain in the United States.

However, neither agency directly addressed questions about the alleged violence or whether Washington had intervened with Equatorial Guinea’s government.

The case presents a serious test for Trump’s third-country deportation strategy: Washington paid millions of dollars to secure a destination, but the deportees’ treatment after arrival has become a source of legal and human-rights scrutiny.

title: First Thing: Banished to alien lands – Trump's secret deportation deals - The Guardian
description:
She is one of thousands of people deported from the US on the back of shadowy deals made with dozens of countries.
The Guardian joined 23 other media organisations in the Deportation Project, a joint investigation coordinated by Forbidden Stories.
Since returning to office in 2025, Donald Trump’s administration has deported more than 25,000 people to countries that are not their own.
The Trump administration has struck 35 deals allowing it to deport migrants and asylum seekers to countries where they often have no connections.
A US federal appeals court ruled on Friday that the Trump administration’s third-country removals policy was unlawful.
text:
Good morning.

After a plane journey in shackles, an Iranian woman found herself in the middle of Africa in a country she did not know existed. She is one of thousands of people deported from the US on the back of shadowy deals made with dozens of countries.

Human rights lawyers describe these so-called third-country national arrangements as part of a “show of force” by the US, intended to discourage migrants and asylum seekers from entering. People from Peru and Colombia have been sent to the Democratic Republic of the Congo. On 20 August, four Cubans, a Brazilian and a Cameroonian refused to disembark in Liberia, and were sent to Equatorial Guinea instead.

The Guardian joined 23 other media organisations in the Deportation Project, a joint investigation coordinated by Forbidden Stories. The consortium reviewed documents and interviewed more than 100 people on the US drive to extinguish unauthorised immigration.

At what scale are third-country deportations happening? Since returning to office in 2025, Donald Trump’s administration has deported more than 25,000 people to countries that are not their own.

Which countries are people being deported to? The Trump administration has struck 35 deals allowing it to deport migrants and asylum seekers to countries where they often have no connections.

Is this legal? A US federal appeals court ruled on Friday that the Trump administration’s third-country removals policy was unlawful. A three-judge panel unanimously agreed that it violated due process. But the government has 90 days to appeal against the court’s decision, and is expected to do so.

European spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against Nato

European intelligence officials have raised the possibility of an imminent Russian test of Nato, with one saying a potential attack could come in a matter of “months, not years”, the Guardian’s Shaun Walker reports.

The warnings come after Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, told parliament that intelligence assessments suggested Russia might launch an attack with drones or missiles on Nato territory in the coming months.

The escalation fears come as the UN general assembly convenes in New York later this week, and amid intensifying airstrikes on both sides of Russia’s war on Ukraine.

How imminent is the threat? Normunds Mežviets, the director general of the VDD, Latvia’s state security service conceded there were signs that Moscow was making preparations for more decisive action in Europe, but said it was not clear whether the plans were simply part of a destabilisation strategy. “It’s still an open question if they have direct and concrete plans or if it’s just within the context of their overall attempts to spread fear and uncertainty in western society,” he said.

Middle East braces for more violence as Iran claims US is planning to renew bombing campaign

Governments across the Middle East are bracing for an escalation of violence after Iran claimed it had received intelligence that the US was preparing for a renewed bombing campaign against it.

Keeping his options open, Trump reportedly told a Fox News reporter “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future” and that the options he was considering were “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal”.

What has Iran said? The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned that if an attack did take place, “all US bases and interests in the region will become targets of continuous, effective and painful attacks without any limitations or considerations”.

What has caused the outburst of sabre-rattling? It appears to have been prompted by attacks on the Saudi capital, Riyadh, by Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. The US largely regards the Houthis as a proxy Iranian force.

In other news …

Friedrich Merz, Germany’s chancellor, has vowed to stay in office, despite heavy losses for his conservatives in two state elections, one to the far right and the other to a leftwing party.

Gavin Newsom, the California governor, has signed off on a package of bills aimed at bolstering election security, including measures to block federal political interference.

Eighteen people have been arrested in association with the assassination of the Haitian president, Jovenel Moïse, who was killed in July 2021, according to US officials.

Starbucks workers say their health insurance premiums have soared this year, in some cases more than doubling, according to a survey conducted by Starbucks Workers United.

Stat of the day: 2.7m more lives could be saved in next pandemic if vaccines are shared more fairly, says report

An extra 2.7 million lives could be saved in the next pandemic if countries share vaccines in a less selfish way, a new study has found – although the death toll in richer countries would rise. Researchers modelling a hypothetical global outbreak of flu found that fast-tracking vaccine development could cut deaths from 58.5m to 23.9m.

Building Power: They fought against datacenters. Now they are running for local offices

A national datacenter revolt – which has built coalitions between environmentalists and Nimbys, conservatives and democratic socialists – is turning some community organizers into political hopefuls, Claire Wang writes. Dozens of datacenter activists are running for offices held by incumbents that they feel have disregarded issues of affordability, environment destructive and the overreach of tech power.

Don’t miss this: Is culture alive?

“Cultural traditions endure because they share a fundamental property with biological organisms. They are alive. Not metaphorically, but literally,” writes Jonathan Loh for the big idea. “I believe that human culture isn’t just an accidental add-on to organic life; rather, it’s a separate expression of life in its own right.”

Climate check: EPA let Bayer pick regulations for destructive weedkiller, documents show

The Environmental Protection Agency allowed Bayer to pick from a menu of regulation options for the controversial and destructive weedkiller dicamba, internal agency documents reveal – then it put Bayer’s choices into a proposed federal rule. The Center for Biological Diversity has brought a lawsuit over the issue.

Last Thing: ‘I got married in it’ – Guardian readers on their favorite thrifted fashion finds

The anti-poverty charity Oxfam is challenging people to avoid buying new clothes for 30 days and choose preloved pieces instead. The Guardian asked readers about their best thrifted finds. “From a distance it looks pink, but as you get closer you realise it’s swirls of pink dots creating an optical illusion,” Alicia said, of her $5 wedding dress.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security’s investigative arm is leading a probe into a federal agent’s shooting of an immigrant from Venezuela in Austin, Texas, on Sunday afternoon.

Protesters immediately gathered at the scene to denounce the latest instance of violence involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, with videos on social media showing them paralyzing traffic. Texas law enforcement was deployed to the scene to respond and attempt to disperse the gathering, CBS Austin reported, detaining multiple protesters and firing pepper balls into the crowds.

“I’m very angry about this,” Austin Mayor Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said in a press conference about the shooting, adding that local police were not involved in the incident, which happened during a traffic stop.

Watson said he was not surprised by ICE’s involvement, given “the nature of ICE and the way ICE is doing its business these days.”

Watson and other Texas Democrats have also called for independent investigations into the incident. James Talarico, who’s campaigning for a U.S. Senate seat, said he was “closely following” the reports and urged a probe that released available footage of the shooting. “Previous incidents have shown that this agency cannot be trusted to report all the facts,” Talarico said in a statement released to the media.

The District Attorney’s Office in Travis County, which includes Austin, requested to partner with city police in the investigation and for the federal government to cooperate in providing access to evidence. It added: “As has occurred in other jurisdictions, it is possible that this incident included violations of state law.”

Rep. Greg Casar (D, Texas) wrote a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and acting ICE director David Venturella seeking a congressional briefing on Sept. 28, and asked the agencies to publicly release all body and dash camera footage from federal officers present at the scene and recorded communications between agents before and after the shooting.

Casar and Watson claimed that ICE activity in Austin has increased in recent weeks amid President Donald Trump’s implementation of his strict anti-immigrant agenda. “It’s a disturbing pattern,” Casar said, “and it has got to stop.”

Here’s what we know so far.

What happened?

The shooting occurred near the intersection of Anderson Square and Research Boulevard in Austin. The Texas Tribune reported that Texas state troopers received a call at around 12:50 p.m. from ICE officials, citing Sheridan Nolen, a spokesperson for the state’s Department of Public Safety. The officials reportedly asked for help to pursue a blue Toyota Corolla.

But Nolen said that before the state troopers arrived, an ICE agent had shot a man, and upon the troopers’ arrival, they treated the driver of the Toyota Corolla.

Austin-Travis County EMS received notification from city police of a shooting around 12:56 p.m. CT, according to its chief Rob Luckritz. They identified a man who sustained a gunshot wound to the torso, with Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis adding that preliminary information pointed to a “small foot pursuit” happening before the shooting.

Authorities then added that the man was transferred to the Dell Seton Medical Center in stable condition.

What do we know about the people involved?

Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, an Austin immigration lawyer who said she had been hired to represent the man who was shot and his wife, identified the man who was shot as a 28-year-old Venezuelan named Wilber Rafael Garces Perez.

The Tribune reported, citing Lincoln-Goldfinch, that Perez had a work permit and had entered the U.S. legally. According to Lincoln-Goldfinch, Perez was delivering for DoorDash when the shooting occurred.

A DHS spokesperson said, without naming Perez, that the Venezuelan immigrant who was shot “illegally entered our country under the Biden Administration and had a final order of removal.” The man is stable and “in federal custody pending removal,” the spokesperson added.

In videos posted to her social media, Lincoln-Goldfinch said Perez’s wife had not been informed of her husband’s condition since and that she was turned away at the hospital’s premises before being informed several hours later that her husband was already in ICE custody.

“If ICE deports him, the key witness to their shooting disappears,” Rep. Casar posted on social media. “He must not be removed from this country, and he must receive proper medical care.”

As for the ICE agent, who has not been publicly identified, when authorities were asked about his whereabouts, Mayor Watson said: “We do not know that. But my hope would be that an agent that’s involved in an officer-involved shooting would not leave the city; certainly not leave the state.”

Is this part of a pattern?

Sunday’s shooting involving federal immigration agents follows another widely reported shooting in July. In Houston, an ICE agent shot and killed 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican national, while conducting a traffic stop. ICE said Salgado Araujo was not the intended target of the operation, though the DHS has claimed, without proof, that Salgado Araujo was in the country illegally and attempted to ram ICE vehicles.

Since Trump’s return to the White House, his Administration has deployed federal agents to Democrat-run cities around the country to carry out the President’s strict immigration agenda, and these agents have been involved in multiple high-profile violent incidents.

Among the first people killed in such operations was 23-year-old U.S. citizen Ruben Ray Martinez. A federal agent fatally shot Martinez in South Padre Island, Texas, on March 15, 2025.

title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico sue Trump administration over White House access
authors: Katelyn  Polantz, Brian Stelter, Tierney Sneed
description:
The three national news outlets President Donald Trump banned from the White House — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — filed a critical First Amendment lawsuit to restore their access.
“Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting,” the news outlets said.
It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters are unable to access their workspaces inside the White House.
After Trump announced he was barring the three outlets from the White House because he didn’t like their coverage, reporters’ press passes to access the White House grounds were deactivated.
The courts have been clear that journalists cannot be prohibited from covering the White House because of what they say or publish in the coverage itself.
text:
The three national news outlets President Donald Trump banned from the White House — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — filed a critical First Amendment lawsuit to restore their access.

The emergency request is set to go before a federal judge in the DC District Court and could result in hearings and legal arguments from the administration as soon as this week.

“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the outlets said in their lawsuit, which is asking the court to act immediately to revive their journalists’ access to the White House.

The lawsuit will allege Trump’s ban violates the First Amendment and the Constitution’s due process protections.

“This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,” the three news organizations said in a joint statement on Monday.

“Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting,” the news outlets said. “Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.”

The standoff is one of the administration’s most high-profile attacks on the press to date, with implications extending far beyond the three banned news outlets. Trump said last Friday, when he announced the ban, that he might add others to the list.

“The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America,” Trump posted to his social media account Monday morning. “It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”

CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters are unable to access their workspaces inside the White House. CNN and MS NOW are also blocked from using their television equipment and camera locations on the grounds.

CNN was removed Monday from pooled coverage responsibilities that are shared by major news outlets. CNN was scheduled to have TV pool duty and travel with the president to New York on Monday.

“The ban inflicts an injury on all news media organizations—which now risk a similar fate if they engage in fact-based, independent reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable,” the outlets said in a request for a temporary restraining order that was filed on Monday.

“And the public at large suffers for however long the unconstitutional ban restricts access to current and complete information about the government.”

CNN has reached out to the White House for comment on the lawsuit.

Some first amendment and legal experts have already widely called the ban unconstitutional and condemned it as abrupt, discriminatory and harmful to the media’s ability to cover national issues.

The lawsuit from the outlets is expected to rely heavily on the vague reasoning for revoking access that Trump gave on Friday, saying he didn’t like “negative stories.”

“If they want to write them, that’s fine. I don’t have to let them into the people’s house,” the President also said.

At least one Trump administration official said in a TV interview Sunday that he believed a Supreme Court opinion from 1965 about the government refusing to validate passports for travel to Cuba would support Trump’s stance.

After Trump announced he was barring the three outlets from the White House because he didn’t like their coverage, reporters’ press passes to access the White House grounds were deactivated.

On Saturday, MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner, CNN reporter Betsy Klein and Politico reporter Cheyenne Haslett each tried to enter the White House grounds to cover news and were denied entry by the Secret Service, which seized their press passes.

Similar prohibitions that Trump and other White House officials have attempted to put on individual reporters or outlets have been rejected by the courts, even recently. The courts have been clear that journalists cannot be prohibited from covering the White House because of what they say or publish in the coverage itself.

A fight over press freedom

The current dispute centers on a First Amendment legal concept known as viewpoint discrimination, since Trump has been explicit about his reasons for wanting to ban certain outlets over coverage he deems “negative.” Courts have forbidden viewpoint discrimination and protected the rights of journalists in case after case.

The DC District Court, where the three news outlets’ case will land on Monday, has several judges who’ve ruled in favor of press freedom and against the Trump administration for discriminatory policies, especially since Trump took office last year.

The law previously set by the federal appellate court in DC has said the White House also can’t revoke press credentials without giving the journalists due process, especially when areas of the White House are accessible to the general press and there isn’t a national security concern.

That case law dates to 1977, when the Secret Service revoked the press pass of Robert Sherrill, a reporter for The Nation. The federal courts in Washington restored it, with the DC Circuit Court of Appeals ruling at the time, “denial of a White House press pass is violative of the first amendment only if it is based upon the content of the journalist’s speech or otherwise discriminates against a class of protected speech.”

“Not only newsmen and the publications for which they write, but also the public at large have an interest protected by the first amendment in assuring that restrictions on newsgathering be no more arduous than necessary, and that individual newsmen not be arbitrarily excluded from sources of information,” the court also wrote.

In Trump’s first term, journalists Jim Acosta, who worked for CNN at the time, and Playboy correspondent Brian Karem had their press passes suspended, triggering lawsuits. In Trump’s second term, The Associated Press was denied access to the Oval Office and Air Force One, also kickstarting litigation.

The courts largely sided with the journalists in every case, based upon the 1977 precedent, though the courts haven’t gone so far to say that White House press pass access can be unfettered.

Monday’s legal filings pointed to the precedent set in the Acosta case to argue that the press badge deactivations under the current ban are unconstitutional.

The First Amendment attorney who represented CNN in court during the Acosta case in 2018, Ted Boutrous, has been brought on board by CNN, MS NOW and Politico for Monday’s lawsuit.

“The President’s ban of CNN, MS NOW and POLITICO from the White House is a direct assault on the First Amendment and a blatant violation of due process. The President has been explicit that this ban is intended to punish reporting he doesn’t like and to intimidate journalists and news organizations covering him and his administration,” Boutrous said in a statement Monday.

“This ban on the free press harms the American people, who are entitled to rigorous, fact-based coverage of the President of the United States,” he added. “The law is on our side across the board, and we look forward to presenting our arguments to the court as soon as possible.”

The three news organizations have emphasized that their coverage of the Trump administration will continue regardless of the access restrictions.

“CNN’s mission to report on the U.S. government will continue regardless of any attempts to restrict physical access to the White House and other government buildings, or any other attempts to impede our journalism,” CNN said in a statement over the weekend.

This story has been updated with additional information.

text:
In brief

The 1st Circuit largely upheld a ruling declaring DHS’s third-country deportation policy unlawful.

The court said migrants facing removal to an unfamiliar third country must receive effective notice and a meaningful opportunity to raise persecution or torture concerns.

The policy concerns migrants who have final removal orders but have received protection against removal to their countries of origin.

The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals has rejected a policy adopted by the Trump administration that allows authorities to rapidly deport migrants to countries other than their own without giving them a chance to raise safety concerns.

Ruling in a case that is likely headed to the Supreme Court, a three-judge panel on Sept. 18 largely upheld a February decision that declared the Department of Homeland Security’s policy unlawful.

The ruling came in a class action filed by migrants subject to deportation orders that has become a key test of what due-process protections the government must provide before removing people to countries with which they have no connection.

“This decision confirms that due process and the protections Congress enacted against persecution and torture cannot be circumvented by putting someone on a plane to a country that was never part of their removal proceedings,” Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said.

Under President Donald Trump, the administration has entered into a series of agreements that have allowed it to send more than 25,000 migrants to at least 29 third countries, in many cases Mexico, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a project run by Refugees International and Human Rights First.

The government is expected to appeal. Earlier in the case, the administration twice convinced the Supreme Court to lift a preliminary injunction protecting migrants’ due-process rights, clearing the way for eight men to be deported to South Sudan.

The administration has also carried out third-country deportations of people to nations including Uganda, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia and the Central African Republic.

DHS General Counsel James Percival posted on X that the policy remains in force because the 1st Circuit’s decision is not yet in effect.

“If you claim fear in your home country, DHS has the right to send you elsewhere,” he said.

Third-country deportations

In March 2025, DHS adopted a policy aimed at addressing people who were subject to final orders of deportation but had been granted protections in immigration court against being sent back to their countries of origin.

The policy would allow migrants to be sent to alternative countries if immigration authorities have credible diplomatic assurances they will not be persecuted or tortured there.

The policy called for only minimal notice before a migrant could be sent to a third country that had not given the State Department such assurances.

U.S. District Court Judge Brian E. Murphy, an appointee of Democratic President Joe Biden, set aside the policy and concluded that it failed to protect migrants’ due-process rights and could lead to their swift deportation to unfamiliar and potentially dangerous countries, without notice.

On appeal, the Trump administration contended that Murphy’s order, if left intact, would usurp its authority to execute potentially thousands of valid orders of deportation to third countries.

But Judge Seth R. Aframe, writing for the 1st Circuit panel, said Murphy adopted a “sensible” interpretation of the immigration law requiring migrants be given a “meaningful” chance to raise any concerns before they are deported.

“DHS’s proposed interpretation would deny access to that protection to a substantial swath of noncitizens who are sent to third countries with no notice of their destination,” Aframe wrote. “We decline to adopt such an interpretation.”

The panel comprised two Biden appointees, including Aframe, and a judge appointed by a Republican president.

However, the 1st Circuit overturned one part of Murphy’s ruling on procedural grounds. It concerned whether the government must first try to deport migrants to countries they have ties to before sending them to third countries.

(Reporting by Nate Raymond in Boston; editing by Sanjeev Miglani and William Mallard)

text:
A federal immigration officer shot and wounded a man in North Austin Sunday, prompting a large protest near Research Boulevard and Anderson Square.

Austin officials said the shooting happened shortly before 1 p.m. during a federal immigration operation. Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said preliminary information indicated there may have been a brief foot pursuit. Austin police were not involved in the shooting.

PREVIOUS COVERAGE | City confirms ICE Officer involved in North Austin shooting, victim in stable condition

The man shot was identified by his attorney as 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a Venezuelan national. Officials said he was shot once in the torso and was in serious but stable condition.

Demonstrators quickly mobilized following reports of the shooting, lining sidewalks, waving Mexican flags and chanting “Abolish ICE.”

“I want to see that ICE agent be charged with attempted murder or murder if the man was killed,” said David Torres with Dare to Struggle. “I want the deportations to stop completely, because these killings, these murders will continue to happen unless the deportation stops completely.”

Tensions escalated as law enforcement used pepper balls to clear protesters from the street and away from the active investigation scene.

Local advocacy groups organized a rapid response, saying people in the community are frightened by what they describe as a recent surge in federal immigration operations.

“There's other ways to deescalate a system, a situation,” Austin protester Rebecca Cruz said. “There is no reason to shoot somebody unless your life is in danger and their life was not in danger. This is something that is becoming an everyday norm in our community, in the immigrant community.”

After law enforcement left the intersection, protesters blocked Research Boulevard and Anderson Square. Traffic backed up along Research Boulevard, with some drivers telling CBS Austin it took as long as 20 minutes to get through the area.

Protesters said the disruption was intended to draw attention from the public and city and state leaders.

When asked whether she was surprised by the size of the crowd, Austin resident Jenna Geueke said, “No. Absolutely not. Just proud. And I think we can use a few more.”

The investigation remains ongoing.

text:
(NewsNation) — The attorney for a man shot by an ICE officer during a pursuit in Austin, Texas, says her client didn’t deserve what happened to him — no matter his immigration status.

“Even if he did have a final order of removal, he did not deserve to be shot in the back of the neck,” attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch said Sunday on “NewsNation Prime.”

The man, identified as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, is in serious but stable condition with a gunshot wound to the torso, according to Austin Police. Lincoln-Goldfinch has described the wound differently, saying she’s seen photos showing he “was shot below his neck in his back.” Garces Perez is from Venezuela.

Lincoln-Goldfinch, who represents Garces Perez and his wife, said he was shot while driving for DoorDash Sunday morning. His wife got a brief call from him around 12:30 p.m.

“I’ve been shot,” he told her, before the line cut off.

Lincoln-Goldfinch said hospital staff repeatedly denied Garces Perez was a patient there, and security removed her and his wife from the property.

“We know that he’s in this hospital. This is his wife. She knows that her husband has been shot,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said she told hospital staff. “Let her see her husband.”

It wasn’t until Austin’s mayor got involved that they learned Garces Perez had been discharged and handed over to ICE custody around 4:30 p.m., she said. Neither Lincoln-Goldfinch nor his wife have spoken to him since his call that morning.

Austin ICE shooting: What is Wilber Garces Perez’s immigration status?

Federal law enforcement sources told NewsNation Garces Perez had a final order of removal and fled from immigration officers before he was shot. The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that Homeland Security Investigations, with help from the FBI, is leading the investigation into the shooting.

“The illegal alien’s condition is stable, and he is in federal custody pending removal,” DHS said, adding that he “illegally entered our country under the Biden administration and had a final order of removal.”

Lincoln-Goldfinch said she couldn’t confirm the account of what led to the shooting but said Garces Perez had entered the country as an asylum seeker.

She said she’s worried about the medical care he’s receiving in ICE custody.

“I’ve been doing immigration law for 20 years in Texas, and I know that my clients don’t receive adequate care when they are in ICE custody,” she said.

Local leaders, including Austin’s mayor and Reps. Joaquin Castro and Greg Casar, have reached out to assist the family, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

text:
Based on his improper use of generative artificial intelligence (genAI), Australia’s Federal Circuit and Family Court (FCFCOA) found it appropriate to issue a personal cost order against a lawyer involved in judicial review proceedings against the minister for immigration and citizenship.

The court denied the judicial review application of the applicant in Dey v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (No 2) [2026] FedCFamC2G 1799.

As the first respondent, the minister applied for costs, including costs against a lawyer involved. In a submission and affidavit filed on 1 March 2026, the lawyer opposed the potential costs order against him personally.

The court identified genAI use in the preparation of the lawyer’s first costs submission and the submission filed in the applicant’s judicial review proceedings. These submissions included

authorities that were hallucinations or that were not an authority for the asserted propositions.

Specifically, after the court asked for clarification, the lawyer acknowledged that six authorities cited in the judicial review submissions were hallucinations, while five authorities cited in the first costs submissions were also hallucinations.

The lawyer also accepted that the minister incurred costs relating to the costs application because of his inappropriate use of genAI in preparing submissions filed on 1 March 2026 and withdrawn on 5 May 2026.

Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia’s orders

The FCFCOA directed the applicant to pay the minister’s costs fixed at $6.7k. The court also ordered the lawyer to pay the minister’s costs fixed at $9.6k.

The court had no reason to doubt that the lawyer’s remorse and apology for improperly using genAI were genuine. The court found it unlikely that the lawyer would repeat such conduct. However, the court considered this a clear case for ordering costs against the lawyer personally.

In the interests of justice and within its inherent supervisory jurisdiction over lawyers, the court decided that its sanctions should also include a public reprimand through naming the lawyer in its reasons and orders.

Lawyer’s use of generative artificial intelligence

The FCFCOA expected lawyers to ensure that the authorities cited in submissions existed, rather than being mere hallucinations of a genAI program, and to satisfy their professional duties and obligations when utilising genAI.

Regarding the lawyer’s improper use of genAI in this case, the court noted that it was the one that identified genAI use in the judicial review and first costs submissions. The court added that it utilised its resources to fact-check, which was unacceptable.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security said Monday it was leading the investigation into the officer involved in a shooting of “an illegal alien from Venezuela” during an operation in Austin, Texas.

In a statement posted online, DHS said the man’s condition was stable, and that he was “in federal custody pending removal.”

The department’s announcement followed confirmations by authorities on Sunday that a federal immigration agent shot and injured a man.

The man was identified as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, of Venezuela, by his attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch.

Lincoln-Goldfinch told NPR he is married to a woman who has legal status to be in the U.S. He called his wife to tell her he had been shot inside his car and was yelling in pain, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

“We were told that he was at this hospital, so we came back and they have run us off the property,” she said, referring to Dell Seton Medical Center in Austin. “We have been informed that if he’s in ICE custody, they will decline to confirm that he’s here. And no one has updated her about his status.”

Austin Councilmember Mike Siegel spoke to NPR from the scene of the shooting, which is just blocks from his home. He said he saw that the man’s car had at least two bullet holes in the passenger side. Photos from the scene confirm that.

At least one person in civilian clothes who appeared to be uninjured was put in handcuffs on the scene, according to video provided by Siegel.

Earlier at a press conference, Austin Mayor Kirk Watson said that Rafael Garces Perez was in serious but stable condition, .

“This is a terrible incident that we were hoping to avoid in our community,” Councilmember Siegel said. “My hope today is that we can investigate what happened, and if an (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) officer committed a crime that they will be fully prosecuted, and then we can hope to restore some semblance of law and order in this country.”

It’s unclear what led to the shooting. The Department of Homeland Security didn’t immediately respond to NPR’s request for comment.

Dozens of community members gathered to protest at the scene of the shooting. This shooting is the latest in a series of violent encounters involving ICE agents.

Mayor Watson said he was angry and upset about the shooting but “not surprised at all.” He said this has happened in other cities like Chicago and Minneapolis where the Department of Homeland Security has conducted big immigration enforcement operations.

The state of Texas has been working closely with the federal government in issues related to immigration. The Texas Department of Public Safety has been working closely with ICE since President Trump took office last year.

Congressman Greg Casar, a Democrat who represents Austin, demanded an independent investigation into Sunday’s shooting.

“Over and over, ICE has shot people and then lied about what happened,” Casar said in a news release, referencing the deadly shooting of Renee Good in Minneapolis earlier this year. Video footage has disproved DHS’s claims that Good was trying to run over ICE agents with her vehicle.

“We can see the lies with our own eyes. We will demand truth, transparency and accountability,” Casar said.

Sunday’s ICE shooting is at least the second to happen this year in Texas.

In July, federal immigration agents in Houston shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old Mexican national father of three.

Salgado Araujo was killed after agents attempted to conduct a traffic stop. He was not the target of the warrant agents were trying to execute.

description:

text:
Immigration was already a hot topic at the federal level ahead of this year’s U.S. Senate race in Maine.

But its significance ballooned after a surge of Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents descended on the Portland and Lewiston areas in January as part of President Donald Trump’s controversial deportation agenda. Six months later, an ICE agent fatally shot and killed a Colombian man living in Biddeford.

The Trump administration’s actions left no doubt about whether the issue would play a major role in the race between U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson.

As part of the Portland Press Herald’s look at the policy areas factoring into the high-profile contest, here’s a deep dive into how the two candidates view immigration.

Jackson answered the questions sent to his campaign, while Collins campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen answered on the senator’s behalf.

ICE’s actions in Maine

Collins, a 73-year-old Caribou native who first won election to the Senate in 1996, and Jackson, a 58-year-old former logger from Allagash who served in the Legislature from 2002 to 2024, clearly differ on ICE and whether the federal agency should exist.

A bevy of masked ICE agents moved into Maine in January as part of what the Trump administration described as “Operation Catch of the Day” to detain the “worst of the worst” criminals in the U.S. illegally. But people without criminal records and those going through the legal asylum process were among the more than 200 people arrested and seized from vehicles. The operation ended after a little more than a week, per a statement from Collins saying she asked the administration to pull back, though ICE agents continue to operate in the state.

Maine came back into the national — and international — spotlight on July 13, when an ICE agent with a checkered job and domestic abuse history shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old man from Colombia with a wife and 3-year-old daughter, not far from his home in Biddeford.

Loved ones and attorneys said Guerrero had moved to the U.S. a few years prior and was authorized to work while his asylum case was pending. Officials confirmed he was not the target of the operation ICE agents were conducting that morning.

State and federal probes into the shooting remain open, with no clear timelines. Both Collins and her Democratic colleagues have called for a transparent investigation into the matter.

Jackson said ICE’s “cruel tactics” led to Guerrero’s death. Collins, the Senate Appropriations Committee chair, responded to what she called a “tragic shooting” by pointing out she had supported $20 million for body cameras for federal agents and $2 million for deescalation training in a budget bill earlier that year. But the agents at the scene in Biddeford had no functioning body cameras, officials said. In August, Collins said all ICE agents in Maine now had body cameras.

The existence of ICE

Though she said “it is clear that ICE needs to improve its performance” following the July shooting, Collins said she supports the existence of ICE due to the work it does that goes “far beyond immigration enforcement.”

Before the fatal shooting, Collins cast a crucial vote in April to pass a Republican-backed measure giving $70 billion to ICE and Border Patrol. U.S. Sens. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky were the only two Republicans to vote against the measure. Murkowski criticized the plan to fund the agencies for three fiscal years instead of one, which she said bypassed the normal appropriations process, which Collins helps oversee.

Collins’ July comments offered a look at her reasoning on funding ICE.

“Eliminating ICE would make our country less safe and endanger the lives and welfare of countless individuals,” Collins said in July.

Jackson, like Sullivan oysterman Graham Platner, whom Jackson replaced on the ballot in July after Platner’s swift downfall amid sexual assault allegations, has called ICE a “rogue agency” that must no longer exist after agents killed multiple people around the country this year.

“(ICE) needs to be dismantled because they give us nothing in this country but heartache and racism,” Jackson said earlier this year.

Funding ICE

Jackson and other Democrats have hammered Collins for that $70 billion vote.

“She had the ability to stop that $70 billion. She had the ability to stop ICE, and she didn’t, because she’s scared of Donald Trump, and she wasn’t going to push back,” Jackson said in August. “As chair of Appropriations, she could have done that, and she didn’t, and so we have a young family that doesn’t have a father today.”

Kernen said Collins “opposed immigration enforcement actions” that Trump pushed for, including ones that turned violent in Minnesota as well as in Maine, because they were “too broad in scope.”

“She believes that individuals who are in this country legally with pending asylum applications and who have not engaged in criminal activity should not be targets for deportation by Immigration and Customs Enforcement,” Kernen said. “Enforcement should be targeted and focused on individuals who are here illegally and have committed crimes.”

Immigration-related policies

In terms of immigration-related policies they would advocate for if elected in November, Jackson said the country needs “comprehensive immigration reform, and federal law enforcement and immigration services that can be trusted — not masked raids and fear.”

Kernen said Collins is “a strong supporter of visa programs, like the H-2B and H-2A programs, that support Maine’s seasonal businesses and farmers.” She also noted Collins has supported Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, as she “does not believe it is fair to penalize individuals who were brought to the United States illegally at a very young age by his or her parents, as long as that person has no criminal record.”

The system to enter the country

Asked about what Congress must do, if anything, to fix or improve the system in which people enter the U.S., Jackson said immigration services “should be handled by a humane, civilian agency that respects due process and keeps families together; serious cross-border crime should be investigated by accountable federal law enforcement.” ICE should get replaced as well, he said.

“We need to secure the border, and we need to return immigration enforcement to a professional government agency that doesn’t target Black and brown people at the whim of Donald Trump,” Jackson said.

Collins, who reiterated her support for ICE earlier this year, believes “we should enforce our immigration laws and secure our borders,” Kernen said.

Kernen also noted Collins has cosponsored the Northern Border Security Enhancement and Review Act with Democratic Sens. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire and Kirsten Gillibrand of New York. The legislation, which awaits a House vote after breezing through the Senate, would require the Department of Homeland Security to complete a threat analysis of the northern border every three years and update its northern border strategy based on the analysis.

Expanding or curtailing asylum

The Trump administration has worked to limit the ability of immigrants to claim asylum, the process in which people fearing persecution in their home nations are given legal protections in the U.S. Asylum approvals have reportedly dropped to their lowest in at least two decades, and the Trump administration has narrowed the scope of how someone can claim asylum or be approved for it.

Jackson noted Maine has a workforce shortage that asylum seekers can help ease.

“Asylum seekers who are in the country legally and following the rules should have access to work permits, which will help them to contribute to the communities where they live,” Jackson said.

Collins did not directly touch on asylum in the responses from her spokesperson. Kernen noted that she has cosponsored the Religious Workforce Protection Act with U.S. Sens. Tim Kaine, D-Virginia, and Jim Risch, R-Idaho, to allow foreign-born religious workers to stay in the U.S. while awaiting permanent residency.

Ending or continuing Temporary Protected Status

Congress and former President George H.W. Bush created the Temporary Protected Status program in 1990 to grant people from certain countries with armed conflict, natural disasters or other extraordinary circumstances the right to temporarily work and live in the U.S. until the federal government deems it safe for them to return to their home countries.

Trump has ended the program, known as TPS, for 13 of the 17 countries under it, including Haiti and Syria, making hundreds of thousands of people who settled in states like Maine face potential deportation. The administration is considering ending TPS for El Salvador as well.

Collins did not answer whether she supports the Trump administration’s moves to end TPS for various countries. Kernen only noted the White House, not Congress, has the power to decide whether countries fall under TPS.

Jackson said the Trump administration “treats TPS like a talking point to show that it’s ‘tough’ on immigration while ignoring the reality of what’s happening around the world.”

“The administration has not demonstrated sound reasons for its TPS decisions and, instead, seems to be targeting countries that the president doesn’t like,” Jackson said. “That’s not good public policy; it’s prejudice backed by executive branch action.”

How Biden and Trump performed on immigration

Asked where they think both former President Joe Biden and Trump fell short on immigration, Jackson said presidents “of both parties have failed to meaningfully reform our immigration system and secure the Southern border.”

“Congress has also failed in its responsibilities,” Jackson said, without elaborating.

Collins feels the Biden administration’s “disastrous open-border policies” resulted in “record levels of illegal border crossings, made Maine and America less safe and allowed cartels to exploit women and children,” Kernen said, who followed that by saying Collins did not support Trump’s immigration enforcement operations if they were “too broad in scope.”

Evolving views on immigration

Lastly, asked how their respective views on immigration have evolved over the years, if at all, Collins did not directly answer the question through Kernen. The spokesperson said Collins believes immigrants “have long been an important part of our country, and many continue to make valuable contributions to our communities.”

Jackson nodded to his role leading a blockade of the Maine-Canada border in the 1990s to protest what he and other northern Maine loggers viewed as landowners and big companies trying to replace them with foreign labor.

“The problem isn’t working people from Canada,” he said. “It’s large landowners, billionaires and corporations who abuse and misuse immigration laws to pit worker against worker and to depress wages for everyone.”

Jackson said the goal “should be for a system that is fair, compassionate and equally enforced.”

“President Trump has taken a broken system and made it much, much worse. It is a policy based on bad economics and cruelty,” Jackson said.

text:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and wounded a man Sunday afternoon in Austin, Texas, local authorities said, and anti-ICE protesters quickly gathered at the scene.

The man was in serious but stable condition at a hospital after being shot once in the torso on the capital city's north side, Austin officials said at a news conference.

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, confirmed the man was in stable condition and “in federal custody pending removal.”

Homeland Security Investigations, with FBI assistance, is investigating “the officer involved shooting of an illegal alien from Venezuela, who illegally entered our country under the Biden administration and had a final order of removal,” the department said in a statement.

City police officers were not involved in the operation or the shooting, which occurred after a traffic stop, Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said while briefing reporters along with the city's mayor and other officials.

Mayor says he wants city's police involved in investigation

Mayor Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said he wants the city's police department to have a role in the investigation so it can provide “clear, third-party eyes” in the process. Watson said he does not think it would be appropriate for ICE to conduct an investigation on its own.

Austin residents have “a right to feel safe in their city,” Watson said. A proper investigation will only enhance credibility, he added.

The chief said there were not many facts she could provide so soon after the incident but added that her department’s special investigation unit was at the scene.

The Texas Department of Public Safety said it received a request from ICE for assistance in a vehicle pursuit around 12:50 p.m. By the time DPS troopers arrived, the shooting had already taken place, the department said in a statement Sunday evening.

Attorney says man shot is from Venezuela

An immigration attorney representing the man’s family identified him as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan man.

Attorney Kate Lincoln Goldfinch said in a video posted to her Instagram account that she believed he had no criminal history and no final order of removal from the U.S., but she later told The Associated Press that she did not know his current immigration status.

The man’s family has struggled to get any information from the hospital about his status or location, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

Just before 7 p.m., the man’s wife was informed by the hospital’s attorney that the man had been released into ICE custody a few hours earlier, Lincoln-Goldfinch wrote in a text to AP.

“No one bothered to update her,” she wrote.

It wasn’t immediately clear if the man remained hospitalized while in ICE custody or if he had been transferred elsewhere.

Protesters turn out at the scene

A dark blue Toyota Corolla was parked under an overpass with damage to its passenger-side door and what appeared to be bullet holes. The car was towed away in the early evening and traffic began moving again.

A large law enforcement presence was present along with a crowd of about a hundred protesters. Some demonstrators cursed at police officers holding riot shields, while others yelled out as passing cars honked in support of the protest. One man held a sign saying, “Nobody is safe” and, on the other side, “ICE Nazi.”

Asked if Austin authorities knew where the involved federal agent is, given that agents have left states after previous shootings nationwide, the mayor said: “We do not know that. But my hope would be that, an agent that’s involved in an officer-involved shooting would not leave the city. Certainly not leave the state.”

The office of Travis County District Attorney José Pompa Garza asked that local police and prosecutors be included in the investigation.

“We further request cooperation from the federal government in giving us access to the evidence,” the DA's office said in a statement Sunday evening.

U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, a Democrat representing parts of Austin, called for transparency as the shooting is investigated.

“It is awful that this horror has come to our doorstep,” Casar told reporters. “For Austin to be safe, ICE should end its surge here.”

ICE enforcement surged around the nation over the summer

The shooting comes as ICE surges enforcement across the country this summer, producing more than 50,000 arrests a month for the first time in its history in July and August.

In July, an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, of Houston, after federal agents driving unmarked vehicles pursued him while he was taking his construction crew to a job site.

Also in July, 25-year-old Johan Sebastián, a Colombian man, was shot by an ICE officer in Maine. The officer is an Army veteran who has struggled with serious mental health issues since early childhood and never should have been given a badge and gun to patrol American streets, several of his close relatives told AP.

The administration’s enforcement efforts were widely condemned last winter after the killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minnesota.

___

Weber reported from Los Angeles and Boone from Boise, Idaho. Associated Press journalists Kimberlee Kruesi in Providence, Rhode Island, and Tim Sullivan in Minneapolis contributed to this report.

“The horror has come to our city: ICE has shot a person in Austin this morning,” Casar said in a statement released Sunday.

“As the facts emerge, I am demanding a full, independent investigation, immediate release of the body camera footage, and accountability for any ICE officer who broke the law,” he said.

RELATED | Federal immigration officer shoots, injures man in Austin, report says

Casar also accused the agency of dishonesty in past shootings, saying, “Over and over, ICE has shot people and then lied about what happened. We can see the lies with our own eyes.”

He said he expects community members to respond peacefully, adding, “Just like Americans have from Minneapolis to Houston, Austinites will speak out peacefully against this deadly mass deportation machine.”

Casar ended his statement by criticizing ICE’s actions nationally: “ICE has been terrorizing our country for far too long. We will not be silent.”

Rep. Joaquin Castro also addressed the incident, calling for the immediate release of body camera footage.

James Talarico has also made a statement regarding the shooting, saying that he and his campaign are following the incident closely.

I am closely following reports of a shooting involving federal immigration officials in Austin," said Talarico in a satement. "Previous incidents have shown that this agency cannot be trusted to report all the facts. We need a full, independent investigation that includes the release of any and all available footage. As we seek further information, my prayers are with those impacted and with the Austin community.

The Bexar County Democrats also released a statement in the aftermath of the shooting, condemning the shooting and demanding accountability.

Enough is enough," said Texas House Democratic Campaign Committee Chair Christina Morales. "ICE has repeatedly been overly aggressive and violent, due to a lack of training and accountability. There must be a full investigation into ICE's lawlessness. We demand answers.

description:
A federal court has permanently blocked the Trump administration from excluding certain lawful permanent residents from federal food assistance and from penalizing Minnesota and other states for failing to implement the disputed restrictions retroactively.
The decision protects lawful permanent residents who previously entered the United States as refugees, received asylum or qualified under other humanitarian immigration categories.
Eligibility and the Five-Year Waiting Period Federal law generally requires many lawful permanent residents to wait five years before becoming eligible for SNAP.
The ruling means Minnesota cannot be fined under the invalidated retroactive deadline and does not have to remove previously protected lawful permanent residents from food assistance based on the rejected interpretation.
Income requirements, immigration classifications and other federal eligibility rules remain in place.
text:
SAINT PAUL, MN (September 21, 2026). A federal court has permanently blocked the Trump administration from excluding certain lawful permanent residents from federal food assistance and from penalizing Minnesota and other states for failing to implement the disputed restrictions retroactively.

The ruling granted summary judgment to Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison and a coalition of attorneys general that challenged the administration’s Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program guidance in November 2025.

The court concluded that the administration’s eligibility interpretation lacked a legal basis and that its retroactive deadline for states was unlawful and arbitrary.

The decision protects lawful permanent residents who previously entered the United States as refugees, received asylum or qualified under other humanitarian immigration categories.

It also prevents the federal government from imposing potentially substantial financial penalties against Minnesota and other states for failing to meet a deadline that the coalition argued had effectively expired before federal officials finished explaining the required changes.

Eligibility and the Five-Year Waiting Period

Federal law generally requires many lawful permanent residents to wait five years before becoming eligible for SNAP. Congress has created exceptions for refugees, people granted asylum and some other humanitarian immigrants.

The administration’s guidance would have applied the waiting period to certain residents who had originally entered through protected humanitarian categories but later obtained permanent-resident status.

The court determined that changing immigration status did not eliminate the eligibility protections Congress provided to those groups.

The lawsuit also challenged federal instructions connected to SNAP eligibility changes contained in the 2025 Republican budget legislation.

The administration later reversed its position on the eligibility of lawful permanent residents but continued to argue that states could be penalized for failing to comply during the disputed grace period.

Friday’s ruling rejected that position and permanently blocked enforcement of the penalties.

Minnesota Joined 22 Other Plaintiffs

The case was led by the attorneys general of New York and Oregon. Minnesota joined California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, North Carolina, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia.

A preliminary injunction issued in December 2025 had temporarily prevented the federal government from enforcing the disputed changes while litigation continued. The new ruling resolves the coalition’s claims in its favor at the trial-court level.

The administration retains the ability to seek appellate review. No appeal had been announced in the Minnesota Attorney General’s September 18 statement.

Practical Consequences for Minnesota

SNAP provides grocery assistance to qualifying households with limited income. Because the program is federally funded but administered through states, abrupt federal eligibility changes can affect both recipients and the state agencies responsible for determining benefits.

The ruling means Minnesota cannot be fined under the invalidated retroactive deadline and does not have to remove previously protected lawful permanent residents from food assistance based on the rejected interpretation.

It also limits the federal government’s ability to use administrative guidance to impose eligibility restrictions not authorized by Congress.

The court’s decision does not expand SNAP eligibility to every noncitizen. Income requirements, immigration classifications and other federal eligibility rules remain in place.

Its central effect is to preserve eligibility for humanitarian immigrants who subsequently became lawful permanent residents and to prevent states from being punished for refusing to implement an unlawful retroactive policy.

description:

Since Trump returned to the White House and launched his campaign against immigration, however, he has struggled to fill positions.
